speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF ESTAB- LISHMENT OF WHEAT FLOUR STOCKPILE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, by leave of the house I should like to make an announcement with regard to the government program for assisting NATO countries to set up strategic stockpiles of wheat flour. Hon. members will recall that on June 1 of last year I informed the house of the government's intention to ask parliament for $10 million for that purpose. I stated at that time that I had made this proposal, in general terms, at the meeting of the heads of the governments of NATO countries in Paris in December, 1957, whereby I suggested the establishment of a food bank amongst the NATO countries for use in the event of any outbreak of hostilities. I expressed at that time the willingness of the Canadian government to play its part in the establishment of such food reserves, and these facts were communicated to the house on July 19, 1958.
Negotiations with the NATO allies took longer than was expected. It was not until April of this year that the first agreement under the program was completed, and on April 26 the Secretary of State for External Affairs informed the house of the conclusion on the preceding day of an agreement with Norway under which Canada would provide 20,000 tons of wheat flour for wartime emergency stockpiling purposes in that country.
I am now able to announce the conclusion on August 5 of an agreement with the United Kingdom under which Canada will provide 30,000 tons of wheat flour later this year for wartime emergency stockpiling in the United Kingdom. Provision has already been made by the house in the supplementary estimates of the Department of External Affairs for the expenditures required under this agreement and the agreement with Norway.
The agreement with the United Kingdom took the form of an exchange of notes between the Secretary of State for External Affairs and the high commissioner for the United Kingdom. These notes set out the terms and conditions under which the flour will be provided by Canada and stored by the United Kingdom. With your leave, sir, I now wish to table copies of the notes, both in English and in French.
The agreement provides that 30,000 tons of flour, suitably packaged for long storage, will be delivered to Canadian seaports to be specified by the government. The United Kingdom will inspect and assume title to the flour at these ports, with all expenses thereafter being borne by the United Kingdom government. They will transport the flour to the United Kingdom, where it will be stored for emergency use should war occur. When it is no longer fit for human consumption it will be replaced by the United Kingdom, so as to maintain the original level of the stockpile at the initial amount.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF ESTAB- LISHMENT OF WHEAT FLOUR STOCKPILE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think it is unfortunate that the NATO organization itself was not able to make arrangements for the establishment on a broad and collective basis of a NATO food bank, an idea which was put forward by the Canadian member of the council I think two and a half years ago.
In view of the impossibility at this time of doing that, I think bilateral arrangements between Canada and NATO members are useful and, as the Prime Minister has pointed out, one such arrangement has been made with Norway. That has been supported in this house, and we also heartily support that which has been proposed with the United Kingdom as a form of mutual economic aid- perhaps in this case modest aid-which is appropriate for Canada and helpful to the countries receiving the assistance.

Mr. Speaker, we in the C.C.F. welcome most warmly the announcement that has just been made by the Prime Minister. Our party has long proposed and supported the principle of a world food bank to be available in case of any emergency throughout the world.
We are most happy that an arrangement has now been made, not only for the establishment of the principle of the world food bank but to provide for its utilization and replacement if it is not called upon. speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the Prime Minister a question of which I have given notice, and I apologize for the length of it. My question is this. subsubtopic: U.S. BASES
speechtext:

TMr. Pearson.]

My information is that there has been no notification to the Canadian government by the United States of the intention of the United States government to vacate the area in question or, indeed, any other area. There has of course been reference in the press to the situation at Fort Pepperrell but there has been no official correspondence in connection therewith, or indeed with the United States government, on any matter arising out of the projected course.
In so far as the lease is concerned, it is a fact that in March the United States embassy informed officers of the Department of External Affairs that the United States government was contemplating the abandonment of the lease covering the Pepperrell air force base. I would point out that the lease agreement provides in article XXI as follows:
The United States may at any time abandon the leased area or part thereof, without thereby incurring any obligation, but shall give to the government of the United Kingdom as long notice as possible and in any case not less than one year of its intention to do so. At the expiration of such notice, the area abandoned shall revert to the lessor. Abandonment shall not be deemed to have occurred in the absence of such notice.
That is the end of the article in question, and as the hon. member knows, in 1953, probably at his request, the question of the reversionary right was referred to the Department of Justice.
In so far as the latter part of the question is concerned, as to whether the government has taken or proposes taking steps, to discuss with the government of Newfoundland the future disposition of these bases, may I say that according to the information that is given me there has been no correspondence between the two governments. There was a reference to this question at the dominion-provincial conference, when the attorney general of Newfoundland pointed out that there were some differences which had arisen. However, the Minister of Finance points out that this was in the private session. None the less the matter was brought to our attention on that occasion, and I am sure I breach no confidentiality of that private session by revealing that fact.
Naturally, when official notice has been received of the amendment within the provisions of the article I have quoted, in due course there will require to be the fullest consultation between the government of Newfoundland and the government of Canada.

Mr. Chairman, when the committee rose last evening I had started my remarks on this item and had referred to what I thought was an unduly rosy picture of the economy of Canada placed on the record by the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I had pointed out that as an example of the active growth of Canada's efforts in the trade promotion field he had drawn a comparison as to the number of trade commissioners or posts abroad between the years 1939 and 1960 as if that were a real achievement when, if you bear in mind the growth of the population of our country in that interval, the facts indicate nothing of the sort. While the trade commissioner service is a splendid one of which all members of the


committee are proud, the picture drawn by the minister was quite imprecise and not in accordance with the facts. The facts are that there has been a very slight growth since 1952, a growth that was no more than inevitable having in mind the growth of our country and the new countries that have gained their independence and come into being in the world.
The minister seemed to have as the theme of his whole speech the idea that Canadian economic prospects for the balance of the year were very good. I want to refer to a few of the statements he made to see if I cannot put the matter into proper perspective. I express the hope that the rosy prospects for the economy for the balance of the year which he indicated will be realized. No one will be happier than I if they are, but at the same time I do not think it is either useful or proper to base a discussion of trade at this time on assessments that are not factual.
For instance, I might refer to the minister's statement that Canada's gross national product is running appreciably above the level of a year ago. If we are to discuss the matter intelligibly the fact that must concern the committee is that the gross national product is running about one third below the increase estimated by the Minister of Finance when he presented the budget to the house over three months ago. That is the situation today. It may be that the Minister of Finance overestimated the increase in the gross national product this year. It may be that he was justified in indicating the increase he did at the time he did, but whatever the reason for the disparity in the figures the fact remains that it appears now that we are not going to achieve the increase indicated by the Minister of Finance at that time.
This fact is just glossed over. It is one that must cause concern to all of us, because the whole budgetary pattern put forward by the Minister of Finance, and presumably the policies of the government, were based on that estimate. The Minister of Trade and Commerce does not deal with that fact at all. He just glosses over the subject with the brief sentence that the gross national product is running appreciably above the level of a year ago. I suppose the words, if one wants to quibble about it, are true, but they give a misleading picture.
Then we come to this matter of employment. The minister said that this year employment was running some 2 per cent above the corresponding period last year. I suppose if you want to quibble about it, those words may be right enough. I did not look up the statistics, but I suspect they are. Again, it does not deal with the problem that most

concerns this committee, and which was debated rather extensively on the labour estimates; I do not wish to reopen that debate at all, but the facts are very simple. The facts are set out in the minister's own publication dated August 2, the Canadian Statistical Review, where it points out that the index of persons without jobs and seeking work fell from 222 in May to 221 in June. Then in the same publication, where it gives the percentage seeking work, it shows for June 6.3 per cent. In a joint publication put out by the minister and the Department of Labour, dated July 19, dealing with the employment situation in June, 1960, the point is made that the June estimate of persons without jobs and seeking work represented 4.6 of the labour force compared with 3.7 per cent in June, 1959.
In other words, there is a labour situation here that causes great concern to all members of the committee, and I am sure that to take an isolated statistic out of the record to show that there are more people working than there were a year ago, without taking any account of the increase in population in the country or any account of the increased labour force, is not the proper way to put this matter forward.
We could go on with the other items in the minister's speech. He continued his attempt to paint this rosy picture by dealing with Canada's output of motor vehicles. He said that Canada's output of motor vehicles so far this year has remained a little above the 1959 level. While that is technically quite true, actually his own publication which we received this morning shows that the increase amounts to some 1,400 vehicles out of a total of some 278,000. You will see that you will have to be really very good at decimals or fractions to work out what a small fraction or percentage it is. There is a very real problem in the motor car industry that is of concern to persons in that business in this country. One of the things that is affecting this industry

of course there are many and this is only one-is the fact that there is a wider variety of models than there were some years ago. A consequence of this is that there is a larger percentage of the component parts of these cars brought into this country than has formerly been the case, and that means that there is more unemployment in that industry than is usual, quite a bit more.
In so far as the motor parts industry is concerned, there is considerably more unemployment in that industry. Actually, employment in the motor parts industry is down to about two thirds of what it was three or four years ago. This industry has been making strong representations and presenting briefs to the government. I do not
Supply-Trade and Commerce agree with some of the solutions offered in the briefs, but in any event no one can read those briefs without being impressed with the seriousness of the situation to the economy of Canada.
The government itself, I think, has been much impressed, if I correctly understood the remarks of the Prime Minister the other day when he announced the appointment of a royal commission to look into that situation. It is significant that once again, with this situation developing rather sharply over the last two years and having reached the acute stage now, the government is offering us a royal commission instead of evolving some policies that would help to meet these problems. While I look forward with interest to the findings of that royal commission, I want to point out to the government once again that they have done exactly the same thing here that they did to the oil and gas industry of this country by procrastination and delay in evolving a policy, and then when the situation became serious appointing a royal commission which will result in more delay. I must say that the appointment of a royal commission is no substitute for the action that the government should have taken by way of enunciating policies over the last two years.
I could go on, for instance, and deal with the minister's statements on the balance of payments. Now, the balance of payments situation in Canada has been of great seriousness. Our unfavourable balance in international payments is very serious for Canada. This subject was debated as the result of an amendment offered on a supply motion by the Leader of the Opposition during this session, and an effort was made by the Opposition to point out the seriousness of the situation. The minister, in dealing with the subject, brought forward no policies to meet it but just brushed it off in this way at page 7672 of Hansard, where he was dealing with the United States:
Even with the growing imbalance on nonmerchandise transactions, Canada's total deficit on current transactions with the United States is $132 million less in the first quarter of 1960 than in the same period three years ago.
This could be true enough. However, he did not point out the real position that we have; a very serious situation developing. In that part of the subject which has to do with bond interest and dividends there has been a sharp increase in the percentage of this imbalance which results from our abnormally heavy payments to foreign holders of bonds and other indebtedness. That perhaps is something that more properly belongs to the Minister of Finance, but there is also another part of it where our situation is worse. There

Supply-Trade and Commerce is that part of it that has to do with the question of freight and shipping charges, where our balance is worsening, and worsening materially.
He does not point out, for instance, the comparative figures when dealing with merchandise exports. He chooses only to deal with merchandise exports, which are only one part of the problem, and merchandise exports to the United States I suppose last year accounted for roughly one quarter of the problem, or one third of the problem. For instance, in his own department's publication, the dominion bureau of statistics report on the estimates of Canadian balance of international payments what was said on this subject was this:
The reduction in the import balance from merchandise trade in the first quarter of 1960 compared with the same period of 1959 was due to a greater rise in exports from the relatively low level in the first quarter of 1959 than occurred in imports.
In other words, in making comparisons we have to bear in mind the nature of the elements that go into the figures making up our exports and imports. He does not point out that we have a situation where, with regard to the imports coming in from the United States, an ever increasing percentage is consumer goods as opposed to capital goods. Those are the kind of problems that are arising.
Actually, on merchandise trade our exports to the United States are up this year, but our imports are also up quite sharply. If you take the six months for which the figures are available-and I recognize and think it is quite improper to pick out very short periods in any of these trade figures; I do not want my remarks interpreted as doing that, because I do not think that is a proper and responsible way of treating trade figures -the facts are that in the first six months of this year, compared with the first six months of last year, there is a sharp increase in the first two months particularly, and in the first quarter. But in the second quarter of this year, in April and June there is a reduction from last year, and a very slight increase in May. Our exports to the United States for the second quarter of this year are down $82.9 million from the same period last year.
As I say, in my opinion three months is too short a period on which to base an argument. All I want to draw from that figure is that there may be a downward trend in our exports to the United States. It is something that will have to be watched very carefully, and it is something that should cause concern to the minister and the members of the committee. It is a very real problem.

While, as I say, I do not want any final conclusion drawn from quarterly figures on export trade, because I do not think it is a long enough term, yet the facts are there. We are discussing these estimates on August 6; we had better have an awareness of the facts as they exist on August 6, and not pick out figures for any past years and use them, when more recent figures are available.
There is one other thing that I want to say about this subject of the unfavourable balance of international payments, and it leads me into another point that I want to develop. The whole picture created by the minister's speech was of a lovely situation for the economy of Canada, and that is not quite the atmosphere in which we should be discussing our trade today. The facts just do not support that picture. Let me illustrate that, for instance, with one example of balance of international payments. The United States has an unfavourable balance of international payments approximately three times as great as ours, but its gross national product is from 12 to 13 times greater. In the light of that fact, our minister does not treat this subject with the seriousness it deserves. He treats it with the lightness that I indicated. But the United States do not treat their problem in that way at all. Anyone following United States publications describing what they have been doing in this field would see evidence of the greatest concern over what they regard as a great problem for their country. We, with a very much more acute problem on the same subject, do not seem to have the same regard for the problem.
If hon. members will turn to the Bank of Canada annual report to the Minister of Finance for the year 1959, they will find on pages 12 and 13 a couple of paragraphs on this subject. After setting out the problem, which is very relevant and very pertinent, they go on to say this, and I will read only part of it. I have given hon. members the reference if they want to read the whole thing. After setting out the nature of the problem in the United States, they go on to say:
United States policy has not sought to restrict the flow of imports for balance of payments reasons, nor to cut the total flow of foreign aid. Rather it has sought to increase exports-by improving competitiveness and strengthening sales efforts, and by pressing for the removal of foreign import restrictions-and to persuade other countries financially able to do so to look after a larger share of the increased foreign aid requirements of underdeveloped countries.
Every trade publication in the United States will give examples of the aggressive methods they are following to attempt to meet their problem in these ways, but we have no such evidence that our government has adopted a Canadian policy to meet a

much greater Canadian problem. That is my criticism. We have not developed the kind of policy we should to meet the more competitive export trade of the United States. We are going to have to compete with them. They are carrying out a more competitive export trade policy, for reasons they consider very valid, yet we are not taking cognizance of the fact that we are trading against our more competitive neighbours. It is something that should be considered, and I would like to know what the Canadian policy is on the subject.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Trade and Commerce; Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I wonder if the hon. member would indicate to the committee what particular United States government action was taken, as opposed to that taken by private enterprise?

Yes, I can indicate some of those. I do not think I have it here but I had an article, concerning their participation in the British Columbia trade fair, and exactly what the government is doing about it.
You will find also, if you carry out a comparative analysis of their treatment of the GATT negotiations, that while we have a team headed by a very able man, we have not as a government backed that up with the kind of negotiations they have carried on with business and industry in their own country and the kind of arrangements they have made for their potential exporters to be at the negotiations, supporting their representatives. We have done none of those things. Their government have circulated a list of items on which they propose to negotiate.
I put a question in the house, as did my leader, in an effort to get that publication. It was supplied to the Canadian government, but it was not thought important enough to be made available to the House of Commons by the Canadian government. It could be bought at the United States publications office for 30 cents. The Canadian government did not think this important enough to circulate it among the members of parliament, and I venture the opinion that very few of them received it. The Canadian Manufacturers Association circulated it to their members in a confidential way, but the government did not do anything.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: It is not a confidential document; it is a public document.

Yes; it can be bought for 30 cents in the United States. As I say, the Canadian Manufacturers Association circulated it in a confidential way to its members, but the Canadian government either did not prepare any such corresponding list for our country, or if they did-and they 79951-0-485
Supply-Trade and Commerce have not told us whether they did or not- they did not make it available. Or if they did prepare one but decided not to make it available to the members of parliament before the team left for the discussions, they did not disclose any reasons for not making it available. It may be that there are reasons; I do not know.
These are some examples, and I could give a great many more. However, the subject is a large one and I do not want to go into it unduly.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Trade and Commerce; Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: I gather the only functions the hon. member refers to are trade fairs and GATT negotiations?

No, they are just examples. There is a great mass of activities where their government and the whole department seem devoted to a solution of this problem and have taken it up as a great new problem. Hon. members will notice the references in their press to other aspects of foreign trade, and so on, trying to get other countries to assume their share of the cost of foreign aid. I leave that point there.
I now want to indicate some other matters which show the atmosphere we are in today. I am one who over the last few years has sought by means of private members' motions and other means to have this government become more aware of the situation in regard to our traditional trade relations with the West Indies. We have had a very long trade relationship with that country. We have a good trade commissioner service there, but we are losing our trade position in that market, and losing it quite rapidly in terms of our percentage of their total trade.
If the minister will look at the figures I think he will find that our share in that total market has slipped to something less than two thirds of what it was over the period of the last few years. That is a rapidly developing area. They are getting their independence, and there is one more step to that end being taken on August 16. I think all Canadian members of parliament welcome the achievement of their independence.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. I am sorry to advise the hon. member that his time has expired.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Carry on.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Does the committee give unanimous consent to the hon. member continuing?
Agreed.

I thank the committee, and I will try not to abuse the courtesy extended to me.

Supply-Trade and Commerce
In any event, in the publication Monetary Times for July of this year there is an extensive number of features on this subject of trade with the West Indies. In fact the minister has written an article in that magazine dealing with this subject. I am glad to see that he is an author now. There is also a very interesting message from the prime minister of the West Indies, Right Hon. Sir Grantley Adams, and I want to quote two paragraphs from the argument he makes in dealing with the status of imports to the West Indies:
Although in actual monetary terms the value of Canadian goods imported into the West Indies has been rising in recent years, this rise has not been proportionately as large as the increase in total imports into the new federation, with the result that Canada's share of the total import trade has actually declined quite substantially.
I think that is an accurate statement on that subject. Then he goes on to talk about the products exported to here, and I want to quote another portion of his remarks. He says:
In pre-war days considerable quantities of citrus fruits, bananas and tomatoes were shipped to Canada in the cold and capacious holds of the Canadian National Steamships and United Fruit Company vessels. Today this particular trade has virtually disappeared, and Canada/West Indies shipping suffers because cargoes are not available in sufficient quantity, a circumstance which in turn has been reflected in the quality of the shipping available.
Well, the Minister of Transport this morning in reply to a question on this subject asked on orders of the day said that our trade was being adequately looked after as far as shipping to the West Indies is concerned. The truth of the matter is that the government wrongly took the Canadian National Steamships out of this trade, and the Minister of Transport must bear the major responsibility for this. He also did it without regard to the significance in timing. They did not have regard to the fact that this federation is just entering into a dynamic period in its development, and that that historical trade of ours promised to develop. By taking off these ships the government is doing something to help us lose our share of that trade instead of helping to increase it. The government has not done anything to help us even hold our share or to provide any alternative shipping method. Indeed, recent figures on the whole question of freight earnings would show how wrong that policy was in addition to its adverse effect on our merchandise trade.
There are other articles which I could quote showing the dynamic development in that federation, particularly in Jamaica, and there is some very good legislation there dealing with the advancement of their export industries. It is not legislation which would be wholly suitable for this country, but it is

legislation which ought to be looked at to see just what can be done by us in this field. Their problems are a little different from ours in some respects, but in any event it is very good legislation on this subject and is something the government would do well to look at. We have no corresponding legislation or policy on this question at all. The government does not advance anything; it just sits back with no policy.
Now I turn to other countries. In the recent period from 1956 to 1959-1 think that is a fair period to take to illustrate my point, but if hon. members want to take other periods they will find figures which show us up in a worse light than these do-our share of total world trade, bearing in mind the growth of the country and the population increase, in percentage figures was some 5.6 per cent. In Germany, however, her share of the world market for the same period increased by 25.6 per cent, five times as much as ours. France increased her trade by some 14.5 per cent and Japan by some 26 per cent. This sharp increase in the share of world trade held by those countries surely indicates that we shall have to develop policies which will be flexible, energetic and appropriate to meet the problems of trade as they arise. The United Kingdom has been developing a very effective trade policy which has placed it in a highly competitive position.
These things are all to the good, but we have to be in a position to maintain our own share of world trade. There is, of course, a good deal of concern felt in Britain about the European common market and the European free trade association. Our own minister dealt with those matters in his remarks, but his treatment of the European common market area, the European economic community, was wholly descriptive. I think he described the situation reasonably well, and I have no quarrel with his description of the situation. It was very interesting, but the hon. gentleman did not enunciate any Canadian policies to meet this change.
We are in a situation where not only are countries in many parts of the world pursuing, as I have shown, active, efficient and energetic trade policies-and some of them are getting a much larger share than we are getting of the increasing world trade- but the European common market and the European free trade association may present us with some very real difficulties here in Canada.
I should like to hear from the minister exactly what Canada's policy is with regard to meeting these problems. The minister mentioned the agricultural policies evolving in Europe, but he did not elaborate. He might

have elaborated on that and given further information as to the effect the entry of the United Kingdom into the outer seven group and her possible relation with the common market area might have on our export of agricultural products to Europe, but the problem is just left in the air.
The hon. gentleman referred also to the announcement made the other day by the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Finance on the subject of the change of O.E.E.C. to O.E.D.C.; the initials I find confusing at times-in any event the enlargement of that group of 18 countries by the inclusion of Canada and the United States. The announcement which was made in the house was of considerable interest, and I should like the minister to have gone further in stating the policy of the government with regard to that development. The announcement by the countries concerned does not seem to lay much stress on the development of trade relations. It may be too early yet to say what will happen, but the announcement as I read it suggests that the question of handling and co-ordinating economic aid to the underdeveloped countries and problems of that sort will be a major concern. I would hope that we as a country would seek to put forward, in addition, the question of the development of trade relationship in this area and that by now we would have worked out a policy in this respect.
I hope we will hear more from the minister before these estimates pass with regard to Canada's policy concerning the new organization for economic co-operation and development and the other European trading groups which are now emerging. I hope he will tell the committee how the government proposes to handle this matter, and make its views known to those bodies.
I could go on. The subject is a wide one. However, it is perhaps not wise to attempt to cover it all. I do appreciate the courtesy of having been permitted to extend my remarks a little. I wish to conclude by stating that I consider that this country has some quite serious economic problems confronting it at the present time both internally, as I think has been indicated many times this session, and externally, as I believe is clearly shown by the unfavourable balance of international payments as well as by the fact that we are having to export in a highly competitive market in addition to having to meet new types of organizations which are developing across the world. While the objectives of these organized trading blocs are wholly proper and desirable, their operation contains some dangers if not carried out in a reasonable way, and we in this country must 79951-0-485i
Supply-Trade and Commerce be prepared to meet these dangers; we must be prepared to put forward our position.
Up to now this has not been done by the government, as I see it. The minister has not enunciated policy with sufficient detail or clarity. Indeed, I get the impression that the government has no policy with regard to the trade questions and related financial and fiscal matters. Either it has no policy or it has not sufficient appreciation of the seriousness of the difficulties, and I hope that before the end of this debate the minister will try to clear up some of these questions.

Both the spokesman for the Liberal party, who has just resumed his seat, and the minister himself began their remarks with a reference to the fine service which had been accomplished by the late deputy minister, Mr. English. My personal knowledge of him was limited, though I recall that he had extremely pleasant manners. However, I have a general understanding that he was an exceptional civil servant and, of course, our party joins in the tribute to his memory paid by the two previous speakers.
I can with much more force contribute a personal commendation to the minister on his present deputy minister. As a trooper in the army for some years I found very few colonels for whom I had much time. In fact the only one I would bother to give a supreme recommendation to was the colonel of our regiment, now deputy minister in this department. He came to our regiment at a time when I think it was in poor shape in terms of morale, and he turned it into a happy and efficient organization with a great deal of pride in itself. I hope he will do the same for the Department of Trade and Commerce if that should be necessary.
It is our view that there is no greater impending crisis in any phase of Canadian affairs than we face in trade. It may be unreasonable for me as an opposition spokesman to sympathize with the government, but I do sympathize with the minister and the government in this field. This sympathy would have a little more force if it could be supported by some understanding that the government itself appreciated the nature of the crisis. None of us expects at this time to have exhortations to export or die. A previous speaker characterized the minister's remarks in introducing this matter as rather mildish pollyanna sentiment. We are pleased to have his assurance that the policy will be kept flexible, that the department is aware of impending trouble, but I would say we should have developing now on the initiation of the minister, and in the next several days, a real national debate on our trade policy. It seems to me there is very great need for one.

Supply-Trade and Commerce
A tremendous number of things are coinciding to make trade a vastly important issue for Canadians, yet the discussion does not have too much coherence or form. One reason may be the optimistic interpretation, in some ways justified, which the government places on the trade figures that are coming in. There are dozens of different starting questions you could introduce in a debate on trade. I think the most controversial one at the present time relates to our agricultural exports. Questions could also be introduced regarding O.E.E.C., GATT, the commonwealth preference situation and indeed the whole tariff situation.
One of the best things that could be done to focus a real debate on trade would be if some political spokesman would come out and campaign for commercial union or unrestricted reciprocity with the United States. I do not say that because I advocate it, but in the early years of this century, around 1911, we did have a national issue raised by this particular question; and with the way our trade is swinging more and more to the United States and with the present imbalance of trade with that country vis-a-vis our exports, it seems to me that commercial union or unrestricted reciprocity is something well worth talking about and considering. I should like to hear from the minister whether his officials have considered it, and what reasons they have given for rejecting it or for going slowly on it as a possible policy.
I hope all hon. members interested in trade have read the two fine pamphlets put out by the Canada-United States committee, one dealing with the growth of trade between Canada and the United States and the other dealing with barriers to trade between the two countries. It seems to me that our future destiny in trade terms so much lies with our United States neighbours that we need to understand and appreciate the situation much more fully than we do. My own sense of what the Canadian people are feeling is that we have a very strong nationalistic desire, if anything, to avoid too close a merger with the United States in trade and other fields, and the government reflected this itself in the last election campaign with the promise of a 15 per cent diversion.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: There was no such promise.

There was an indication that the government was interested in a 15 per cent diversion. This latent nationalism which crops up once in a while is a great barrier to any serious discussion of commercial union or unrestricted reciprocity. I recommend to hon. members a book by Ronald B. Mac-Pherson published a year ago on "Tariffs, Markets and Economic Progress". On page 36


the author goes into the possibilities of Canada and the United States entering into planned stages that would lead in effect to commercial union. He points out the practical difficulties in the way and the great danger to Canada because of our relatively small size in relation to the sheer dynamism and scope of the United States market.
Whatever the case, it seems to me that if we cannot have unrestricted reciprocity or commercial union or planned stages leading to free trade with the United States as a policy on the part of politicians, the whole issue of United States trade needs to be gone into and studied much more fully, not least because of this latent antagonism that exists in Canada toward United States influences.
I can give one concrete example from my own particular region, which the minister may know is a great exporter of basic raw materials. Whenever I visit my constituency almost everyone I talk to points to all the tons of iron ore being shipped down to United States steel mills. They ask why we let the Yanks process this raw material, why we do not do it ourselves. I can give them all kinds of answers about the cost, the lack of limestone and the inability to find markets for direct reduction ore, but their point of view reflects both a nationalism and an antagonism toward seeing so much of our basic raw material going to the United States for processing, and often a recognition that the material comes back to us in the form of manufactured goods at a much higher value.
I endeavour to point out to these people that we would be completely dead in northwestern Ontario if it were not for the United States. We have nine pulp and paper mills, the bulk of whose production goes into the United States market. It forms part of the very substantial export business we have, the newsprint, the kraft paper, the sulphite that goes into the United States market. I tremble with apprehension, as I think any hon. member does if the economy of his area is closely linked with the United States economy, that the people in the area will not be too rough or tough with respect to the United States, because the danger of losing those sales and markets is enough to frighten anybody.
I bring up this point because I think it is time we took a close look at our relations with the United States, to see whether the time has come for us to try to back off from going in any deeper; or, if we are going to be remorselessly drawn in, because of the superior drive of their economy in terms of using our raw materials and as our great trading partner, it seems to me we ought to know the dangers and know just how far we can go before our national identity and our control of our whole economy disappears.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Trade and Commerce; Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, would the hon. member indicate whether he is now reversing his previous statement, in which he advocated free trade?

One of the difficulties in trying to present alternatives in this chamber or in any political forum is that people want to say, "You are for this or for that". All I am suggesting is that one of the great discussions that should be taking place in Canada at the present time is on our trading relationship with the United States. I feel that one way it could be crystallized would be if some political group or the minister could indicate where they stood on a feature of our past such as commercial union or unrestricted reciprocity.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, may I ask the hon. member a question? Is that not a function of the hon. member, to indicate his stand? It is not just a matter of raising questions about where the government stands. Let the hon. member state his position.

As the minister knows, our party is having a convention next week which will be dealing with issues like this. I cannot particularly be a pace setter. My own personal feeling is that our destiny is linked inexorably with the United States. I have looked to the Liberal party. Last year I heard the leader of that party say the party was for an eventual movement to an Atlantic free trade area. This is all very nice and sweet. This ultimately would have the effect of free trade or commercial union with the United States; at least that would be part of the picture. But I am suggesting that commercial union is something we may get whether we like it or not if present trends continue, and if we encounter the difficulties in the world trade picture that it seems to me are apparent, especially in relation to the European situation.
In many respects the Canadian internal economy has seen its most fantastic growth in terms of manufacturing and in terms of the service industries, but in the export field the service industries do not provide you with anything unless you want to count what they may provide for tourists who come here. Our manufacturing industries are not getting a remarkably increasing share of our export trade to countries other than the United States. I think in the present position of agricultural abundance in the world and with world markets glutted with raw materials of every kind, Canada must look toward her manufacturing industries to expand, not only to employ the idle labour we have in Canada, or to process further our raw materials and increase their value and so earn more for
Supply-Trade and Commerce us in exports, but also to gain foreign capital with which we can finance our way in the world markets.
I do not believe Canada can continue indefinitely to mine her resources and have her high standard of living. We must industrialize and export more manufactured products whose higher value will enable us to continue the present expansion of our economy and maintain what I, as a socialist looking at what is a quasi-private enterprise economy, agree has been a fantastic growth in the past decade. It seems to me that if Canada is to export manufactured goods it is natural that she should look for markets in those areas of the world which are now less developed and are at present entering a phase of industrial expansion. Asia, Africa, South America, Central America and the Caribbean areas come to mind.
From this point of view it is particularly disturbing for us to see that over recent years Canadian exports to all these areas have been slowly and progressively shrinking in relation to our other export patterns, especially in relation to the United States. While Canada's trade with these areas has never been very large, nevertheless it has been very important inasmuch as it provides a market for a disproportionately large percentage of our highly manufactured goods such as processed foods, drugs, chemicals, clothing, paper products, machinery and appliances. For example, the West Indies federation, which in dollar terms ranks thirteenth amongst Canada's trading partners, ranks fourth as a market for highly processed and manufactured goods.
I think one of the main reasons why we will have difficulty in moving into this particular area is our failure to provide credit facilities. This is one important factor limiting Canadian sales in these expanding areas. Canada lacks adequate credit facilities with which to finance sales of machinery and capital equipment. Countries such as Brazil, Mexico and India lack foreign exchange, in particular they lack dollars. Contracts for large projects and capital equipment for these countries are not let so much on price as on the credit terms which the seller can provide.
Many instances of sales having been lost to Canadian firms for lack of adequate credit facilities are apparent in scanning the financial papers. A recent move on the part of a group of Montreal businessmen to form their own export bank and thus remedy the difficulty has not, as far as I know, had any government support. It seems to have died for lack of adequate backing. Surely the Department of Trade and Commerce should be moving into this field. I should like to

Supply-Trade and; Commerce point out to the minister a paragraph in an article by one of my favourite economic writers, Andrew Shonfield, found in the Observer of July 17, 1960. At the end of an article dealing with Mr. Macmillan's concern over the British export situation he says:
Certainly the government will not obtain the results that we need without spending more money, not just on prodding businessmen, but in giving them favours-like the benefit of some free advertising in foreign markets. There is also a case for adopting a more lavish policy in subsidizing export market research and other costly preliminaries, which a firm has to undertake before it can hope to sell anything abroad.
After all, if we are prepared to devote public money to support firms which set up factories in particular areas where they serve the public interest, why be coy about applying the same method to induce firms to start selling in export markets?
As I understand the situation, the British are ahead of us in supporting long term credit arrangements for their exporters. Here is one of the leading economists of Great Britain advocating that they go even further in accepting responsibility because of the vital importance of exports. It seems to me that the Export Credit Insurance Corporation set-up is a very good one, but the government should have been considering extending it, especially from the point of view of providing credit on a long term basis. We feel there is a desperate need for large amounts of capital at reasonable terms over periods of 10 to 15 years to finance long term capital programs in these underdeveloped areas, which would lead to the sale of Canadian products, especially manufactured products with a high engineering content, and perhaps the provision of engineering assistance.
Another area where we would appreciate more information from the minister has to do with the question of tariff barriers to Canadian trade. It seems to me that as our country becomes more and more industrialized it is natural that Canada in the first instance will look toward her natural and traditional trading areas for markets for her manufactured goods, the United States and the United Kingdom. But the United States and the United Kingdom originally set up their tariff schedules so as to admit freely those raw materials needed for their own industries, and at the same time they have given protection to those industries against competition from imports, including our products. Thus Canada now finds that she is locked out of these markets for manufactured goods.
It is significant to compare the changes that have taken place. The booklet, "Barriers to Trade", issued by the Canadian-American committee has this to say on pages 6 and 7:
On the United States free list, there are 110 specific items for which there were imports of $100,000 or more from Canada in 1957. In contrast, there are over 500 no-duty items in the Canadian tariff lists for which there were imports of $100,000 from the United States in 1957.
That is a very strong argument for reciprocity. On page 7 there is the following:
The general tendency in both the United States and Canada over the past 30 years has been for the free items to decline both in number and in relative importance. Between 1929 and 1931, duty free United States imports from Canada averaged about four fifths of total imports as compared to only three fifths today. A similar shrinking of the relative importance of free items among United States exports to Canada is observable, although the drop is less marked. The fact that the United States tariff act has not been revised in almost 30 years doubtless accounts for the persistence of some items, such as bread, which has recently begun to offer strong competition to some domestic producers near the Canadian border.
These quotations point up our weakness vis-a-vis the United States in getting manufactured items over their tariffs and into their trade economy. It is also significant to note with respect to Canada's trade with the United Kingdom during 1959 that less than 20 per cent of Canadian exports received any tariff preference whatsoever, whereas 80 per cent of United Kingdom exports to Canada came in under preferential tariff treatment. As an example, British automobiles enjoy a tariff preference of 17 per cent over all others, including United States automobiles. This would seem to point up the tariff duties that face our products in the United States and the United Kingdom where strong, sharp and persistent negotiations and pressure seem to be necessary in order to give our manufacturers a chance.
One of the problems we face so far as exporting is concerned is the subsidies given by foreign countries to promote exports. Many countries give tax write-offs and special concessions to industries to encourage their export trade. For example, Germany and Britain both give tax rebates to shipping companies. On page 74 of this booklet published by the Canadian-American committee you have this paragraph:
The Canadian nickel industry is understandably concerned about government subsidies to the Freeport Sulphur Company, which processes Cuban ore. The U.S. government has invested roughly six million dollars in a plant at Braithwaite, Louisiana, which was sold to Freeport in March 1959 for $236,455. Under a purchase contract, the government is obligated to buy 271 million pounds of nickel at 75 cents a pound from Freeport Sulphur-
Then later, on page 75, we have this:
U.S. fluorspar production has, for many years, been greatly exceeded by imports. The major sources of supply are Mexico, Spain, Italy and West Germany. Domestic mines are unable to supply the vastly expanded requirements of United States industries, and the government has resorted

to a combination of tariff protection and purchase programs to stimulate output. Thus, while domestic acid grade fluorspar was quoted in trade journals at about $50 per short ton during 1958, the government was paying $53 under stockpile contracts; and the industry was further sheltered from foreign competition by a tariff of $2.10.
These are two examples of what other countries, countries which are our trading partners, do to protect and develop exports. These actions, incidentally, while not contravening the letter of GATT are certainly doing so in the spirit by providing subsidies for exports. Action along similar lines which is embarrassing us is the dumping duty being levied against Canadian chemicals in the United States and the United Kingdom. We would like to hear from the minister what that situation is and what products in those two markets have had dumping duties levied against them-I refer to Canadian chemical production-and what is the scale of the matter.
Another bar to Canadian trade abroad is the restrictive series of health and sanitation regulations which apply to a good many pharmaceutical lines. It is almost impossible to get approval to market ethical drugs and vaccines in the United Kingdom and the United States. The same thing applies to some varieties of processed foods. These laws are used to delay and discourage our exports.
The final form of bureaucratic stonewalling that is encountered in the administration of customs tariffs is the fact that it may take months or even years to obtain a tariff ruling on a new product that Canada may want to put into the British or the United States market. The whole future of our trade, of course, is complicated by regional associations. It has now become accepted that more and more regional customs unions are being formed in the western nations, and so far Canada does not seem seriously interested in getting into any of them. We have the European common market, the European free trade area, the Central American customs union and the South American customs union, and they are all either well on their way or under consideration at the present time.
The ones that are of chief importance to Canada are the two European blocs, that is the European common market and the European free trade area. So far the European common market has been setting the pace, to such an extent that if you pick up any of the British economic journals it is apparent that Britain is in a complete snit about the developments that are taking place there. I do not mean that they are not prepared to take part, but it has been an in and out game in so far as the British are concerned. I understand that the minister
Supply-Trade and Commerce cannot give us any idea on how we are going to stand in the British market in the light of the possibilities of the European free trade area and the European common market. I take it from this that the British have been less than kind to us in the negotiations that have taken place.
For example, I should like to know what assurances the British were prepared to give when Mr. Maudling was over here. I have followed British affairs fairly closely, and there is a lot of maudlin sentiment about the commonwealth; but my impression from my reading has been that there is a switch away from any hope that Britain can stay away from the European blocs. She has made some kind of rapprochement with the European common market and if she does enter that bloc it may not be a case of the devil take the commonwealth and the devil take Canada, but we are likely to get much less consideration than we would have obtained a year ago.
The ultimate goal of the European common market is to eliminate tariff barriers between the members of the community, while presenting a uniform tariff to all outsiders. This means a gradual lowering of some high tariffs against outsiders but also a raising of some tariffs for low tariff countries such as Holland and Germany, both important customers for Canadian goods. So far we have had two 10 per cent tariff cuts in the European common market, the first on January 1, 1959 and the second on July 1, 1960. The embarrassing feature of raising the tariffs has been put off until January 1, 1961, which will enable the whole situation to be talked over at the GATT meetings in Geneva this fall. At present opinion differs as to what may take place in the very fluid situation.
I noticed that the parliamentary secretary was guying the Liberal spokesman about what examples of United States action he could point out which would indicate that the United States was considering this matter more seriously than Canada. Well, I could refer the parliamentary secretary to the Economist for July 23, 1960, which contains an article entitled "Tussle Over Tariffs".

Besides this the administration has (for the first time) drawn up a list of those products on which it hopes to win concessions-a list that runs practically the full gamut of the trade statistics. Most officials are taking pains to point out that America must have some attractive concessions to offer if it is to get more leg room in foreign markets, although the secretary of commerce, Mr. Meuller, has asserted that America should, on this occasion, get rather more than it gives in recognition of its past generosities over tariffs.
I would like to ask the minister, are we going to ask tor more than we are going to give because of past generosity? Have we a short list of parallel points? Have we had any hearings with exporters or manufacturers, with anyone, about the concessions that we are prepared to give in Canada? I would like to hear about this, because these meetings are coming up shortly and I imagine the minister's officials are to appear before them. If this is not action by the United States, I am very surprised. It seems to me very pragmatic action. What are we doing of a comparable kind? I think that is a fair question to ask the minister. It seems to me that Canada's interest stems from the fact that at present 70 per cent of her exports to E.E.C. go into Germany, a low tariff country, which according to the schedule is due to raise some of her tariffs on January 1, 1961. It is also of interest to note that 70 per cent of our exports to E.E.C., which are

mainly agricultural and raw materials, enter under rates negotiated by Canada and bound against increases by individual countries. What happens to them if we get a general increase in tariffs by E.E.C. on January 1, 1961?
When you look at the E.F.T.A. situation you also find that on July 1, 1960 the first cut of 20 per cent in the tariff rates between members of E.F.T.A. took place. So far this is not serious but with future reductions Canadian agricultural and forest products, which now enjoy a preference on the British market, will be faced with free entry goods from Denmark, Sweden, etc., and everyone knows that the Danes are very good at agriculture and that the Swedes have very high quality forest products. This is bound to affect Canadian exports, though to what extent it is difficult to say. I would like to know whether the minister can hazard some estimate as to how we are going to be affected in these particular fields of agriculture and lumber products in the E.F.T.A. area by the competition that will come from Denmark and Sweden.
The minister is more than aware of the relative state of confusion between E.E.C. and E.F.T.A., and it is almost anyone's guess whether these two will get together and form a larger European free trade area. I would take it from what the minister said that he would encourage this development if at all possible, perhaps with the idea that with the larger group-not six or seven, but a larger group of 13-it may be possible for the government to get a better deal or better arrangement in so far as Canadian goods are concerned. At present talks are going on between Germany and the United Kingdom on these matters. I wonder whether the minister has anything to report on these conversations. The United States is certainly showing concern over these groupings, and she is showing concern following a great deal of encouragement that she gave in this direction earlier.
At the very least the future of the European situation is uncertain, and our uncertainty is almost doubled or tripled by the fact that we are not in on the thing except through GATT and the negotiations that are going to take place there.
It is always interesting to reflect-and members of our party have done this before -that there is provision under NATO for economic co-operation, although this clause has never really been put into effect.
One of the questions I would like to ask the minister is whether he feels that Canada can only obtain tariff concessions for Canadian exporters through giving tariff concessions to countries importing into Canada.

In the face of all this one wonders whether Canada has bargained away all her concessions already. Certainly all manner of goods obtain free or near free access to the Canadian market, to the extent that severe pressure has been put on various sectors of our economy. We only have to look at textiles, rubber goods or automobiles, to name a few. I could flip through the first 14 or 15 pages of the minister's annual report and see potential weaknesses all over the place because of the competition and the fact that we seem to have perhaps let barriers down too far.

speechtext: I wonder if the hon. member would permit a question. Is he advocating that there should be tariff increases?

The parliamentary secretary knows very well that I am not, but certainly it has to be considered by the government. The textile industry is in very bad shape; the automobile industry is in very bad shape, or it shows possibilities of getting into a very poor condition. The manufacturers of rubber goods seem to need protection; any protection there seems necessary. For an individual member to stand up and say we want higher tariffs it seems to me is a most retrograde step, but surely our commercial policy in these fields needs some analysis and some prediction on the part of the minister to tell us where we are going to go if we have already bargained away our position, as seems to be indicated by the fact that domestic industries are in trouble. What steps is the minister going to take to remedy this situation?
I think Canada might usefully look at Australia's example. Here we have a country in a similar stage of development, but which has used quotas, tariffs, and licensing arrangements to so restrict imports that it has become profitable for many foreign industries to set up manufacturing or assembly plants there. For instance, there is a Volkswagen plant in Australia. While Canada's automobile industry has been contracting since the war, about six new assembly and manufacturing plants have been set up in Australia to serve that particular market. Australia has used tariff protection to establish these industries, while Canada has fallen into the position where an ever increasing share of cars on the road are imported from overseas.
If I understand the hon. member correctly, he has recommended that we follow Australia's example, which is increasing tariffs. Is that his view?

I am suggesting that we look at what the Australians have done, because they have been able to get German and 79951-0-486

I say that if Australia has been able to achieve this, it might be an example to us in some way. They still seem to be able to sell their raw materials and agricultural goods on the world market, despite the fact that they have these barriers.
In conclusion, I suggest that Canada is not pushing her weight in world trade councils. We are always in the unenviable position of trailing along as "me too" in the wake of British or United States proposals. For a nation which boasts of the world's highest per capita trade volume this is a pathetic situation indeed. There are many avenues open to rectify this situation, but the present government is unable or unwilling to do so.
First, Canada should press for modification of GATT and call for more scrupulous adherence to the principles of the treaty by member nations.
Second, she should make more extensive use of the many provisions in GATT that give a country freedom in making unilateral tariff decisions, such as parts 18 and 29 which provide for the protection of infant industries in a new country in the process of industrialization. Third, some provision over and above the Export Credit Insurance Corporation should be made for financing the export of Canadian products to underdeveloped countries which lack the dollars for outright purchases. It seems to me that these are all steps the government should consider and eventually will have to consider.
I have tried in my reading on trade in recent weeks to get some understanding. I talked to one financial expert on one of the prominent Canadian newspapers very much interested in trade, and he said that one of the things the government needs to do is to boot some of our manufacturers on the fanny and get them to sell outside. I take it that the trade missions announced by the minister are one move in that direction.
I think another step the government should take is what I referred to earlier-and it is almost a national psychological situation-and that is the need to make us aware of all the problems involved in our trade and the desperate need for us to expand and to look at our trade situation with the Americans.
One point I want to conclude on is that I have been disappointed in the fact that one of the largest elements in any manufacturing situation has not taken more aggressive lead

Supply-Trade and Commerce in looking at our trade situation. I am referring here to our own Canadian Labour Congress. I was always very much impressed with the brief which the Canadian Labour Congress presents to the government, but it does seem to me that we should expect more initiative from this particular organization in the field of trade, even as a defensive measure; because one of the great arguments of people who might think they have a deep enmity against the labour movement is that the reason we are not getting a greater share of the export trade is because of our very high labour costs. Another argument which is raised is that the reason so many imports come into this country is that we cannot produce these kinds of products at a low enough cost because again our labour costs are too high.
If I were to make an appeal it would not be to the minister or to the government; it would be to the organized labour of this country to take a look at our trade situation and see if there is not some way they can take the initiative in dispelling some of the rumours and doubts about their own role in our cost pattern, and also to see whether we cannot blast our way into more markets and sell more Canadian manufactured products and in that way employ more Canadian workers.

Mr. Chairman, I regret that my remarks on the minister's estimates at this time must be of a critical nature. My remarks will be chiefly in connection with the Canadian wheat board, which is administered by the Department of Trade and Commerce.
I am aware that under the Canadian Wheat Board Act the Canadian wheat board is given very wide powers pertaining to the delivery and merchandising of western wheat, oats and barley. I also realize that these powers were given to the wheat board by parliament. However, I feel that the present officials of the Canadian wheat board are not carrying out the policies of this government; and I wish to stress that point. They have also become too complacent in their attitude to their duties as members of that board. I might say here that the powers they have been given are too wide to be administered by bureaucrats.
Mr. Chairman, my criticism can be broken down into two fields, marketing and politics. My chief concern has to do with the marketing of western grain both in our domestic market and in our foreign markets, and I am deeply concerned with our diminishing grain markets. The political field can be considered minor and I would suggest the difficulty can easily be rectified, but I will deal with that aspect of my remarks at the conclusion of what I have to say.


In regard to the marketing of western grain, I feel that the present officials of the board are not doing the job they are capable of doing, or possibly I should say that they should be capable of doing. I would draw your attention, Mr. Chairman, to the grain trade year book, which indicates that in some foreign markets Canada's grain sales were reduced by a considerable amount during the grain years 1958-59 from those of the previous grain year. An article which appeared on August 4 in the Western Producer stated that the visible supply of western grain has increased by 42 million bushels this week over the same week last year. I have also before me a table which shows that during the past year Russia exported 40 million bushels of wheat to western European countries, and many of these countries were former customers of Canada.
It is to be noted that Canadian wheat sales to the Netherlands dropped from 21 million bushels in 1957-58 to 7 million bushels in 1958-59. That is an actual decline of 14 million bushels in one year in sales to one of our most valuable customers. During that same period, 1958-59, Russia sold to the Netherlands almost 10 million bushels of wheat.
This situation was brought to the attention of the officials of the wheat board during the consideration of their report by the agriculture committee, but I am not satisfied with the replies to the questions which were put to them. I would ask, how does your department account for this situation? Would you suggest it is a matter of price or availability of grade required, or both? I am quite sure that the producers I represent will have an answer to the board if they contend that the question is availability, when the farmers' bins are full of millions of bushels of unsold grain. In fact, daily on the prairies at the present time many thousands of bushels of wheat are being bartered for feed at any rate.
It is also to be noted that Sweden purchased over two million bushels of wheat from Russia during 1958-59 and practically nothing from Canada during that same period. May I ask what efforts were made by the Canadian wheat board to capture any part of this Swedish market? France, also a former customer of Canada, did not purchase wheat from us in 1957-58, as she was an exporter at that time. In 1958-59 how was Russia able to sell France eight million bushels to our one million, when France again became an importer and was in the market for foreign wheat?
It is also noted that sales by Canada to the United Kingdom dropped in the past year by four million bushels, and Russia

has apparently gained this additional market. Has the increase in the tariff on British woollens contributed to fewer wheat sales to the United Kingdom? During the 20-year period prior to 1939 the United Kingdom imports, combined with their domestic production, averaged 278 million bushels. Canadian sales to the United Kingdom during the same period averaged 141 million bushels, or slightly over 50 per cent of the United Kingdom's consumption. After the second world war, from 1945 to 1949 during the British-Canadian wheat agreement, our share of the United Kingdom market was increased to 56 per cent or an average yearly export to the United Kingdom of slightly over 150 million bushels. From 1953 to 1959 our average yearly sales to the United Kingdom dropped to 100 million bushels or only 36 per cent of their total market. What was the reason for this decrease in sales to the United Kingdom when the United Kingdom imports of wheat and flour were greater during the last six years than the preceding four years?
In the past it was apparently the custom of the United Kingdom buyer to carry stocks of Canadian wheat in the United Kingdom. It would appear that this no longer happens, but rather that the Canadian farmer and taxpayer are expected to carry this load. What caused this trend? Was it a result of present policies of the Canadian wheat board?
During the 20-year period prior to 1939 the annual average world trade in wheat was approximately 660 million bushels. Canadian export sales during the same period were 240 million bushels, or 35 per cent of the market. During the period 1947 to 1959 world wheat trade averaged 993 million bushels annually. Canada's average export sales over the same period were 277 million bushels, or 27 per cent of the world market. What is the reason that the Canadian officials charged with the responsibility for wheat sales did not capture a larger percentage of this increased world market?

I am aware that those who do not agree with my remarks will charge that I am trying to interfere with the orderly system of marketing of western grain. I hasten to say that if such a system solves or will solve the problem of the western grain surplus, then I will support it wholeheartedly. On the other hand, if the present orderly system of marketing works to the disadvantage of the western grain producers whom I represent, then I suggest that some of the conditions in this system should be changed.
I am not advocating that the orderly system of marketing should be discarded. I believe I am offering evidence that proves that the way it is functioning at the present time can lead to only one result, the loss of further grain markets for our producers. It is essential that we avoid this downward pattern.

Figures taken from the annual statements of the Canadian wheat board show that the cost of handling a bushel of wheat has progressively increased from 4.8 cents in 1943-44 to 16.8 cents in 1957-58. The officials of the board have stated that the administrative cost of handling a bushel of wheat is three eighths of a cent; therefore we must assume that the additional 16 cents of cost is attributable to storage and interest, which is deducted from the farmers' return per bushel.
I suggest that if there was more flexibility in the pricing policy of the wheat board, at least within the 16 cent range paid for storage and interest, there would have been more sales of wheat as well as some relief in respect to the storage problem of the western grain producer. It is no secret in the west that the elevator companies are enjoying substantial profits from these storage charges. I contend that this is revenue derived from the sale of grain which should be going directly into the pockets of the farmers rather than into the coffers of the elevator companies.
In an articled entitled "Where Your Tax Money Really Goes", published in the Financial Post of July 30, 1960, reference is made to the fact that grain storage subsidies did not begin until 1956, and that they will total $424.7 million in five fiscal years. It

appears to me that the present policies of the wheat board are working to the advantage of the elevator companies rather than the farmers whose interests, as I mentioned before, they were designed to protect.
Time does not permit me to deal at length with our coarse grain markets. The same criticism I have offered as to the board's handling of our wheat problem applies equally in the case of oats and barley, with these added observations. The present price of oats would indicate that there is a demand for this grain. Oats at the time I prepared this information were worth roughly 20 cents per bushel more than the farmers' initial payment. Why then was there an apparent shortage at the lakehead when the demand was there? Was this a result of poor planning, or of lack of foresight on the part of our officials? If a commodity is not available when the demand is presented, I suggest this is one way to discourage potential buyers, and certainly it is not in the interests of the producers trying to diversify their production to include crops which are in demand on foreign markets. Why has there been no supplemental quota for oats this year as in former years? I contend that the present wheat board appears not to concern itself with what the current demand might be. If they were abreast of the times they would have means of ascertaining the demands of foreign buyers and would have the produce readily available for any potential sale.
What effort has the Canadian wheat board made to capture the market for barley that presently exists in the United States? Would the minister not agree that if this market, which is available, could be captured, more of our wheat producers could convert their production to barley, thus cutting down our problems of surplus wheat? I understand that one hon. member has had representations made to him with respect to the possibility of a Peruvian market for our western barley. Why has that not been investigated? I could cite specific cases where my constituents, in my opinion, have been discouraged from producing barley as the result of routine handling of their problem by the officials of the wheat board. I wish to stress the point that the present wheat board officials appear to be too complacent and apathetic. They lack imagination and initiative to do the job they are charged with doing and, I state again, are not following out the policies of this government.
