Supply-Trade and Commerce certain provincial candidates of the party. Before I elaborate on the particulars I wish to remind the minister of the statement of one of his present cabinet colleagues, when he said that if you allow trained civil servants to take over, you get a bureaucracy and democracy ceases to exist. The taxpayer and the public are still important and deserve protection against the encroachment of bureaucracy, but politicians and public servants sometimes forget this fact.
I would also suggest that if civil servants desire to remain above politics, they should not use the powers of their office, in either word or deed, to influence public opinion in favour of one party or another. I believe some officials of the Canadian wheat board deliberately used the powers of their office on the eve of the last Saskatchewan provincial election to influence the voters in one constituency of my riding. They called in the R.C.M.P. to assist them to investigate a great number of producers for infractions under the wheat board act. This action undoubtedly contributed to the defeat of the candidate representing the Conservative party in that area.
I do not condone the infractions of the wheat board act on the part of the persons concerned. On the other hand, I do not agree with conditions of a law which educate people to be lawbreakers. This observation may be straying from the point in question and perhaps would be better as a topic for later discussion when the wheat board act comes up for review. It is common knowledge in the west that in certain areas, in order to survive and be able to purchase the necessities of life, many farmers take chances and market their grain in any manner which presents itself, regardless of whether or not the courts would regard it as legal. Grain is the only produce they have for sale or exchange for family needs. It has been known to the wheat board for some years that these infractions were taking place and were not prevalent in just one area, but rather were scattered widely over all the spring wheat district.
I ask the minister, in view of the hundreds of complaints the wheat board have stated they have received over the years in connection with these infractions, why did the officials choose this particular time and area for an active physical investigation, if it was not for political purposes? I would remind the minister that as the employees of the Canadian wheat board do not come under the Civil Service Act, steps should be taken to assure this committee and members of all political parties that such action will not be indulged in again by officials of the government.

Last year, we spent $1.46 billion beyond our means and this has been the situation ever since the Conservative government has been in power. In the last four years, the Department of Trade and Commerce, or the government of Canada, has put us into debt to the tune of nearly $4 billion.
At that rate, for how many more years can Canada run deeper into debt before panic breaks out?
We in this country note a state of alarming crisis which hints at a change of administration, which would be a solution, or else we will have to surrender our assets, and our economy and our policies will then be controlled by the U.S.A.
Mr. Chairman, in support of his predictions with regard to an increase in our production,


the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill), makes much ado about U.S. capital investment in Canada. He piles up figures and statistics to present a confusing picture of the real economic situation, which, however, reveals entirely artificial circumstances.
It is true that until 1957, Canada enjoyed a record development, as expressed by the rapid increase in our capital goods. That is why the Minister of Trade and Commerce feels so confident. But there are quite a few economists, including the governor of the Bank of Canada, who consider this one-sided development-if I may so describe it as a cause for concern, for it is not in keeping with the trends of our export trade or consumer market.
We may wonder today whether Canada has not borrowed abroad more than it can afford, thus shouldering a heavy financial liability which we can only meet by increasing our exports and our domestic marketing.
Yet, our imports have been increasing while our exports failed to rise in the same proportion.
In the textile field, for instance, in 1959, there was a record demand for 555 million yards of cotton goods in this country. This was an increase of 15 per cent over the previous year. Of that quantity, 326 million yards were imported in 1959, including 240 million yards from the United States alone. It was the first time in Canadian history that the United States supplied us with more than we had produced ourselves. We imported 28 million yards more than in 1958, while we produced 14 million less.
The portion of Canadian production which was left to our industries then fell to 41 per cent last year, while it was 45 per cent in 1958, and 51 per cent in 1956.
In 1959, our imports from Japan were 56 per cent greater than in 1958.
Our imports from Hong Kong, which amounted to $3.1 million in 1958 increased to $6 million in 1959. Furthermore, according to D.B.S. figures, our imports from Hong Kong have amounted to $2.3 million in the first three months of 1960. At this rate, our imports from Hong Kong should amount to something like $10 million by the end of 1960. They are a greater threat to our Canadian ready-to-wear industry than our imports from Japan, because there are no quotas in that British colony.
The same thing is happening in the field of synthetic fibres.

Our imports have gone up 18 per cent in 1959 as compared to 1958. In fact, in 1959, we imported 32 million yards of fabric from the United States; this was a million yards more than in 1958, and 5 million more yards than in 1956.
We also imported 1.3 million yards of fabric from Great Britain in 1959, as against only a million yards in 1958.
Again during the same year, in 1959, we imported 6.5 million yards of synthetic fibres from Japan; this was 2 million yards more than in 1958.
The proportion of those products used for our domestic requirements dropped from 75 to 69 per cent between 1956 and 1959, a decrease of 6 per cent.
The situation in the textile production as a whole may be summed up as follows:
In 1956, the production of our mills reached 394 million linear yards of fabric, while it dropped to 342 million yards in 1959, a decrease of 52 million yards within 4 years.
In 1956 our mills were producing 55 per cent of our domestic consumption, whereas in 1959 they were producing only 47 per cent.
In 1956, the three main sectors of primary textile products were employing 51,340 persons, but in 1959 that number was down to 43,097, a decrease of 8,253.
There, Mr. Chairman, you have a picture of the Conservative government's constribu-tion to the cause of our textile industry: lowered production in our mills, higher imports and, as a result, increased unemployment.
What is happening in the textile industry is also happening in other sectors of our economy. It is the same in the case of footwear. In 1959, we imported 5,598,734 pairs of shoes of all kinds, i.e. 44.1 per cent more than the 3,886,242 pairs imported in 1958. In 1959, footwear imports, from Japan only, increased by 144 per cent, as compared to those of 1958.
We are importing 26 per cent of our chemical products requirements, whereas the United States are importing only 2 per cent, Great Britain 10 per cent and Japan 7 per cent.
In 1956, the automobile industry was employing 35,099 persons and was producing 467,864 cars, while in 1959, the number of employees went down to 33,160, and the number of cars to 368,587.
Our 1959 imports reached $243,088,000, representing 122,340 cars. Mr. Chairman, all
Supply-Trade and Commerce sectors of the manufacturing industry in Canada are feeling the disastrous consequences of imports. The situation has reached the point where action must be taken at once, if we want the future of this country to rest on a greater and stronger manufacturing industry.
In so far as textile industry is concerned, the government has already in its statutes an act which may be applied, to put a stop to the flow of cotton imports subsidized by the United States, and to determine satisfactory prices for Japanese import products; but the government does not seem to wish to apply that act. And yet, before the election, the Conservatives had solemnly promised to solve, once and for all, the problems of our manufacturing industry, especially those of the textile industry.

Mr. Chairman, we have witnessed an amazing revelation this afternoon. We have heard two speeches from the Liberal party which are without doubt the most dismal exposition of Liberal policy that I have ever heard. We have heard a bullheaded speech from the hon. member for Port Arthur. He went ahead and contradicted everything he said last session about what we should do. He then changed his views and said he was not a leader and could not state the best policy.
We have had no Liberal policy at all, and we have had no C.C.F. policy at all. It would appear that they have not been able to put anything forward. We had scholarly dissertations on the problems of trade from the hon. member for Ottawa West and the hon. member for Port Arthur. We have just finished hearing the best high tariff speech I have ever heard in this house. I hope the Sifton press in western Canada takes particular note of that speech.
I am very sorry, sir, that the two-headed free trader from Windsor is not in the house this afternoon. Certainly we should be given the benefit of knowing which of the two roads he has taken. On one occasion he is the best free trader this country has ever known, but when it comes to his home town industry he loses his free trade instincts almost immediately. We have seen him get up in this chamber twice in the same day, at one moment he is a free trader and the next moment he is a high protection man and we have to protect this automobile industry in his home town of Windsor. I admire his ability to stick up for his constituents, but certainly he should have a little bit of consistency, particularly since I have just finished reading an article in one of the maritime

papers which forecasts that he is going to lead the Liberal party next year.
I suggest that we in western Canada have had enough of glib-tongued Liberals who have been infiltrating boards and other organizations out there. We heard the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek this afternoon. We have had enough of glib-tongued Liberals. We intend to keep the sincerity that has been shown by our present Prime Minister. We do not intend to see western Canada sold down the river as it has been sold for the last 25 years by a combination of the Liberal party and the Sifton press, and for no other reason. They have put forward great stories about free trade in western Canada, but they are not sincere in their presentations, nor are they making any presentations on behalf of the people of western Canada.
They talk about agriculture. We heard agriculture discussed by the hon. member for Port Arthur. Unfortunately for him, the hon. member for Ottawa West did not have too much to say; he was going around in circles. What about agriculture? There are many agricultural problems. We have heard the Leader of the Opposition and the hon. member for Essex East talk about this British free trade offer, but what they have not said and what has not been publicized enough is the fact that the British free trade offer was a manufacturing free trade offer which would exclude agricultural products. Let the hon. member for Essex East come to the west and say that we should have British free trade in manufactured products and leave out agricultural products.
The hon. member for Port Arthur spoke about what is going to happen to our trade with the outer seven. He should know that agricultural products in the main are excluded from the agreements of the outer seven. He is a man who maintains that he is an expert as an individual M.P. in this house. I suggest that he should go back and do a little further studying, particularly with regard to trade in agricultural products.
We need, and we have been given leadership by the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the Minister of Finance. Reference was made to what is happening in Europe, and here the hon. member for Port Arthur should do a little studying on how this inner six came about. If he did, he would realize immediately that this is a political ambition of the United States. He should do more reading in those little books he had there, and a little further study on the matter. Then he would realize that we are being given better leadership in Canada right now than the United States are getting in their endeavours to recapture their lost markets. I had the privilege of meeting and talking
Supply-Trade and Commerce with people in the United States who were vitally concerned about this matter.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I would like to bring this up, because the hon. member for Ottawa West and the hon. member for Drummond-Arthabaska made some passing reference to it. It is the question of manufacturing automobiles in Canada. Where does the blame lie for the failure of the automobile manufacturing industry in Canada? It lies right with the management of these automobile companies, and the trade unions. That is where the blame lies. They should not try to pass it off on this government.
The hon. member for Port Arthur made one sensible suggestion. He wanted to see the Canadian Labour Congress do a little more. He did not go far enough. We want to see our Canadian trade unions become Cana-dianized, move their headquarters back into Canada and move their funds into Canada. To do that would help our industries. One of the ways they could have helped was by advising the management of the automobile industry. Everybody else in the streets could see it coming. We did not want the longer and flashier cars; we wanted something in which we could get around; we wanted transportation, but they were not supplying it. This goes back to the failure of the trade unions and to the management, in the automobile industry, and there the blame lies, and only there. The government is not supposed to go out and lead these people by the hand.
Then, Mr. Chairman, I want to come to something much nearer home as far as I am concerned. The hon. member for Ottawa West had the nerve to say something with regard to gas and oil. Where is the Liberal policy on gas and oil? It is down the drain, and has been for years. I have not heard one realistic speech from the Liberal party on gas and oil since 1958, when I came to this house; not one. To say that this government procrastinated and delayed in regard to the oil and gas industry is a complete untruth. Nothing is further from the truth, and that was absolute nonsense that he was spouting. What about the oil and gas industry? Because of this government, because of the Borden commission, because we went about it systematically, we did not delay for one minute the export of gas from this country. Anybody who studies the situation with regard to the gas industry would realize that. This was not delayed, but it gave to Canada stability in our oil industry; it gave us a program to work on. Only yesterday the United States authorized a second large group of gas import permits for California, Oregon and the southwest United States. This, Mr. Chairman, is going to mean a major capital

Supply-Trade and Commerce expansion program in the province of Alberta which will spread over into the province of British Columbia, to the tune of $400 million within the next year and a half.
What was the Liberal gas policy? The Liberal policy was that we could not export any gas. I have not heard any other policy, and that is the one the Liberals are now advocating, that we should not export any gas. Yet we are to have the benefit of $400 million in capital construction because of this one step. I am happy to say that a substantial amount of that construction will be taking place in my constituency.
We will move on, Mr. Chairman, to oil. Where is their policy on oil? What are they going to do with oil? Where are these free traders of the country? Free traders down the drain, and the Sifton press along with them. We have an oil industry in Alberta which is producing at 55 per cent or less of capacity, yet these people are talking about free trade. I would ask them about Quebec. We can, on an equitable basis, put oil into the Montreal area. Any time we are given the protection we can do so at no cost to the residents of Quebec. This rumour which has been spread around by the Liberal party primarily is to the effect that if we build a pipe line to Montreal the people in Quebec will have to pay higher prices for their gasoline and petroleum products, which is absolute nonsense and a betrayal of western Canada again as they have betrayed us over the years. We are 20 years behind because of the Liberal party and for no other reason.
Then the hon. member for Drummond-Arthabaska talked about Japan. He said our imports from Japan went up by about 30 per cent but he did not mention that our exports to Japan went up 40 per cent and that most of these exports came from western Canada. I am a little tired of listening to this two-headed monster over here who will do anything to gain a vote and who has spread rumours around western Canada. They have been supported by the Sifton press and the Wesson press to sell Saskatchewan, Manitoba and Alberta down the river again. It will be a sorry day for western Canada if the Liberals ever regain power in this country.
The hon. member for Port Arthur says that he has nine pulp mills in his area. I have only one but I do know that one pulp mill is very grateful to the Minister of Finance and his budget for the effect of the exchange on the dollar because it has made a great difference to the lumber people who are now able to get back into the United States market.
As I have said, we have heard no statement of policy at all on the part of the Liberal party this afternoon and we certainly


have not had anything from the C.C.F. I can understand the position of the C.C.F. because they are having a convention next week, and if the hon. member for Port Arthur did what he told the rest of us to do, where would he be? He would be in a rather silly looking situation.
There is one other important problem I want to speak on for a moment and it has to do with oilseeds, and particularly with rapeseed oil. I take nothing from the hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort who initiated the action on rapeseed and has done everything in this house to get it going; and two or three weeks ago we saw the amazing spectacle of the hon. member for Assiniboia running around trying to jump on the band wagon. Where was he when this case was being presented to the board of transport commissioners?
The hon. member for Assiniboia did not even know what rapeseed was. He has been spreading other stories in Canada about the decison of the board of transport commissioners, and I think it should be put on the record so all can see exactly what the position was. As I understand it, two of the members of the board said that it was a grain within the meaning of the act and should be given Crowsnest pass statutory rates. The chairman of the board said no, that it was a grain, but not within the meaning of the 1925 statute. So we have a point of law which has to be settled and that is why the cabinet cannot act. It cannot act until such time as the Supreme Court of Canada has decided this point of law. Then the cabinet can act. So let us get that straight, especially the hon. member for Assiniboia and the hon. member for Essex East.
Now I want to say a few words with regard to rapeseed oil because each year we import into Canada about $56 million worth of oilseeds. I am talking of edible oilseeds and I exclude flax seed oil. Primarily these imports consist of soybean oil, palm oil and cottonseed oil. They are the major ones but there is also a certain amount of corn oil being imported as well. For the record, rape-seed oil is as good an oil for all the purposes for which vegetable oils are used as any of these other oils. Some propaganda has been floated around in the quasi-medical field that corn oil was the last ditch in preventing arteriosclerosis or hardening of the arteries and coronary heart disease. That is not a fact and the advertising which the manufacturers of corn oil margarine were starting in the United States had to be withdrawn because of provisions in the food and drug act in the United States. I understand that

the food and drugs people in Canada are going to consider this question.
Although it is rather a detailed chemical explanation, rapeseed oil is every bit as good as corn oil medically, scientifically or otherwise. I would hope that our trade commissioners and the Department of Trade and Commerce will give to this fledgling industry and thus to our western agriculture a solution for diversification to rapeseed and will give their support to every measure which will help promote the use of rape-seed oil, and also sunflower seed oil which we also grow in Canada, and enable them to be used for purposes for which other vegetable oils are used.
Those are the few things I wanted to put on the record. I am getting a little tired, as I have said, of the Sifton press and the Wesson press in western Canada promoting this great idea of the Liberal free trade nonsense. We have heard such nonsense from the hon. member for Drummond-Arthabaska and the hon. member for Essex East, who runs off in one direction one day and in another direction the next, depending who he is speaking to in the galleries or at home. I would suggest to him that he look at this very closely, and if he wants to be honest he will readily admit that we have never had a government in Canada which has done more for our trade than the present one.

Mr. Chairman, the prosperity of Canada is undoubtedly coupled and measured by the amount of business we do with other nations. We cannot live and prosper without foreign trade. We must sell to other countries the products of our great forests, the iron ore, the nickel and the copper of our mines, the grain from our farms and the fish from our lakes and oceans. We must therefore be in a position to bargain with other countries, countries that need and want these products. Indeed, there are signposts all over the world which indicate the desire for the goods we produce, but somehow we seem to have lost the initiative in trade and we are slipping in world markets.
I think one of the reasons for the deficiencies in trade with other nations is the protectionist tendency of our government. The tariff on woollens is a shining example of a bad calculation which has increased the [DOT]cost of clothing to the Canadian consumer. Take the case of the Australian trade agreement which, according to the publication The Economist, was threatened because of the Canadian government's insistence on protecting a handful of Canadian sheep raisers and therefore tariff negotiations are going to
Supply-Trade and Commerce be clouded by the government's reluctance to make a dent in its own protection.
No nation has ever enriched itself by putting up barriers against trade or instituting high tariffs. The possible exception is the United States, but they had a sufficient consuming power within their own borders to ensure their prosperity. We sadly lack population and for several generations to come we will not be able to afford the luxury of high tariffs.
The Leader of the Official Opposition has on many occasions suggested that consideration and study should be given to a North Atlantic free trade area with a view to achieving tariff reductions among its members, in stages and not necessarily all at once, when for practical purposes that could not be achieved immediately in one jump. Ten years ago he made a statement to the effect that the time was ripe for Canada to explore the possible advantages of a free trade association of the North Atlantic nations, a fulfilment of the economic vision of NATO, and he emphasized his thought with these words: "No vision less than this will do''. No one in this house can successfully deny today that these words so eloquently expressed in 1950 are even more appropriate today than they were 10 years ago.
I do not wish to pretend to instruct the experts in the civil service for whom I have the highest regard, but it does seem to me that a study could be made of the practices which have been successfully adopted by western European countries. The countries of western Europe have been remarkably successful in selling all over the world, including to the nations of the communist blocs of Europe and Asia.
It should be obvious to everyone that 18 million people cannot consume more than a fraction of the wheat, pulp and paper products, metals and fishery products which we produce and that unless a more vigorous immigration policy is adopted several decades will pass before we can smugly sit back and consume what we produce.
Protection by means of quotas and tariffs can only provide a very temporary and very small level of prosperity for a very few in Canada. This relief will benefit only a few thousand Canadians while the rest of the Canadian population would suffer because tariffs will always produce a higher cost of living. Let us take a leaf from Britain whose international trade experience and know-how is vastly superior than that of our government. The government of that country announced recently that it will consider joining two of western Europe's economic organizations. The impact of this action on the part of Britain may be a little hard

It is true that a part of this $800 million was due to commonwealth preference. What would happen if Britain joined the European market and abandoned the preference? This is something to worry about.
Professor Walter Hallstein, president of the commission of the European economic community, speaking to the committee of chambers of commerce and of common markets in Great Britain last February, as reported in the April issue of the NATO letter said, and I quote:
Trade policy is of enormous importance, not only to ourselves and our community but also to our partners in Europe, in the North Atlantic area, and in the developing regions of the world. I was very struck, a few weeks ago, by a statement made by the British president of the board of trade when he was speaking in New York. Mr. Maudling had occasion to underline the significance of trade policy-and of a liberal trade policy- for the peaceful development of our countries and for their hopes of competitive co-existence with the communist dominated nations. "The objective of our trade policies", he said, "must be twofold; first, to strengthen our own economies, and secondly, to use this economic strength to help others."
Further on he continued:
In a world which is rapidly shrinking, it seems to me vital that while we are striving to avoid in Europe the mistakes which were made by past generations, we must above all not repeat those same mistakes on the wider scale of our Atlantic trade relations. During the past 30 years, American trade policy has undergone a remarkable evolution in the direction of liberalization and multilateralization; and it is in the interest of us all, that this evolution should continue. Our own policy must be liberal, and it must be such as to enable others to continue in liberal policies. It is very important, at this stage, when America is recovering still from a short but sharp recession, and when many people are worried about the state of her reserves situation, that we in Europe give no encouragement to those who demand more protection for her industries and her currency.
I am very glad to say that both the European community and the United Kingdom have accepted the famous proposals made by Mr. Dillon for a substantial reduction of tariff barriers to be negotiated in GATT. This in itself will have the effect of further reducing the external tariff of the European community, and we have even proposed that this round of negotiations be followed by a further round to make a real and continuing attack upon trade barriers in the free world as a whole.
While there may be instances where some protection is necessary to give an infant industry a start, I regard tariffs as a protection against progress; they only weaken industry to the point of delaying necessary changes to meet competition which in the end are bound to be made soon or later.
The interprovincial farm union council have also expressed themselves in terms of favouring the free trade offer made by Britain two years ago. This may not be feasible now


unless we join Britain in the free trade area and the Scandinavian countries of the outer seven. However, Canada could possibly become a willing negotiator between the two blocs and thus achieve a wider free trade movement with tariffs and quota reduced progressively in order to allow our industries to adapt themselves to a new trade climate which in the end would be beneficial to all concerned.
Here I would like to put on the record a resolution by the Manitoba federation of Liberal women passed at their last annual meeting. It reads:
Whereas Canada is dependent upon the export market for one quarter to one third of her national income;
Whereas tariffs raise prices of essential consumer goods, and
Whereas high tariffs restrict trade and tend to impair goodwill among nations,
Therefore be it resolved that the Manitoba federation of Liberal women in annual meeting assembled being of the opinion that increases in tariffs are harmful to Canada because of her need to export goods and services, urges the government of Canada to reduce rather than increase our present tariffs.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Trade and Commerce; Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: Would the hon. member permit a question. Does the hon. member agree with that resolution?

Yes, 100 per cent. It is being widely reported that sales of surplus food to Europe which have gone on since world war II are taken over from Canada by French wheat, Dutch dairy and Danish bacon products. Sales of raw materials are lumber from Scandinavia, uranium from the Congo and coal from France.
The question is, what is Canada's trade policy? Are we going to stand idly by when we see markets which were once considered Canada's own preserves being invaded by the more aggressive selling policies of other nations? Until three years ago Canada was always in the forefront of the world wide effort to reduce barriers to trade. I fear that we no longer occupy that position. I submit that the government take steps to return to that position before other essential export markets are diminished or lost. May I repeat what every schoolboy understands, that with every tariff increase an increase in living and production costs ensues.
A very significant explanation of an unfavourable trade balance is one furnished by an editorial in the Gazette of July 12. It is a simple illustration that trade deficits mean also a deficit in many jobs. I quote:
Unemployment, of course, has various causes. But one of the causes is seen in the trading deficit. For the deficits do not show merely that Canadians bought more abroad than they were able to sell; it means that they helped to keep people

in other countries in employment, while they helped to put people in their own country out of employment.
Canada must increase the volume of her exports. But one kind of export is very undesirable; it is the export of jobs. It has been suggested that if a job had some sort of physical shape-if it was, say, the size of a telephone booth-every time that Canadians went into trading deficits they would be exporting so many jobs. Big orders, or many smaller orders together, might make up quite a shipload.
The whole matter could be made real if Canadians could go down to their harbour fronts and see these jobs, each the size of a telephone booth, being picked up and carried on board to be sent away. All this would be taking place before their eyes while hundreds of thousands of Canadians need jobs at home.
It would certainly make those deficit figures more vivid if they could be thought of in this way. An adverse balance of trade is not an adverse balance of trading dollars; it is an adverse balance of jobs. It is not only a matter of giving work to the Canadian unemployed, important as that certainly is, but whenever anyone has a job in Canada, all Canadians benefit. By working the worker makes work for others. He helps increase the demands for goods and services and he helps share the tax load. Whenever jobs are shipped abroad Canada ships away those things it needs most. No asset is as precious as a job, to the individual or to the nation.
Are we doing enough to encourage manufacturing of the things that should be considered essential Canadian products? I should like to point out that most of our souvenirs of Canada which are usually purchased by tourists are made in the United States or in Japan. Consider a tourist entering Canada for a holiday and while here going shopping for souvenirs to take home to his family and friends. What does he buy? Indian dolls, Indian heads carved in wood and images of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. Do they bear the stamp "made in Canada"? Not at all. The stamp reads "made in Japan". Souvenirs should be made of products from the countries they are sold in, made by the people of that country. To be worth calling them Canadian souvenirs, an industry could be built here. To be successful it might require a little encouragement from the Department of Trade and Commerce.
The minister made reference to the automobile industry about which I want to say a word or two. The impression has been created that the Canadian automobile industry is sick and is fast deteriorating. Such an assumption is erroneous and nothing could be further from the truth. The industry employs some 50,000 workers and has a production value of close to $1J billion. It is true that the imported small cars have taken a good slice of the car market and I
Supply-Trade and Commerce presume that because of the inroad made by the small European car in the Canadian market the government has appointed Dean Bladen to investigate the situation. We wish him well. I am sure that the professor, who is just as qualified as any one can be to look into the economic problems of the industry in general, will now try to find a means to improve the competitive position of the Canadian automobile manufacturers. Let us hope that the distinguished investigator will come up with a satisfactory answer.
Our Canadian manufacturers are now in the process of changing over to new models and the plants will soon be in production of 1961 models. I have so much faith in the ability of their executives that I for one have no doubt that in the end the answer will be provided not by professors but by those whose energy and know-how have built up one of the major industries and employers of labour in this country, and whose faith in the destiny of Canada has never flagged.
Within a month or two the 1961 Canadian manufactured automobiles will make their appearance on the streets and highways of Canada, and I recommend that prospective purchasers of motor cars take a look at these Canadian creations before buying any automobile. I am confident that the verdict will be an improvement in the role of Canadian-made cars. If the government really wants to help the industry, it should consider the immediate removal of the 7J per cent excise tax on motor cars.
Hear, hear; long overdue.

My opinion is that the elimination of this obnoxious tax would do more to revive the industry than any other single government action, and I will be very much surprised if the one-man royal commission does not make the removal of the excise tax on motor cars one of its first recommendations.

Mr. Chairman, I do not intend to have much to say at this time. I think I have expressed my views many times in connection with trade, tariffs and quotas, but at this time I should like to ask the Minister of Trade and Commerce how his department arrives at fair market values for import and export purposes.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: May I tell the hon. member that that is determined by the hon. Minister of National Revenue.

That may be but I
should like to finish my remarks and the minister can then answer. I do not wish to refer to figures too much but I have some

Supply-Trade and Commerce here in connection with the importation of electronic tubes. I do not wish to appear as being opposed to Japanese imports but in some respects I do not think the figures used for imports and exports do justice to our country.
I understand that the declared value of electronic tubes, the value that is accepted by Canada for import purposes, is 31 cents apiece. Yet figures have been made available by the Japanese minister of international trade and industry indicating a value of 60 cents apiece. There is a vast difference between the figure we are apparently using and the figure representing the actual cost in Japan. We apparently use the figure of 31 cents and the actual cost in Japan is something like 60 cents. I also have a figure here supplied by the electronics industry of Canada whose representatives spent four or five months in Japan going into the matter and who came up with a figure of 60.3 cents. Therefore the minister can see that this is a matter which should receive serious consideration.
Perhaps someone may say, what does it prove if the figures are different? I would point out that we are going through a period when foreign trade is most competitive and we hear continually that Japan is buying much more from Canada than we buy from that country. If these figures are correct and we are completely out of line with respect to our valuation of goods that we purchase from Japan, then it may be that on the basis of using correct figures we are buying more from Japan than that country is buying from us.
Another matter I should like to bring to the attention of the minister concerns goods shipped in bulk from Japan to the United States where they are boxed for merchandising and then transshipped into Canada. I have followed this matter through with the Department of National Revenue and I find that even though the goods are manufactured in Japan and transshipped from the United States into Canada they enter Canada as exports from the United States, not exports from Japan. Therefore, this is another instance where the figures we apparently use are completely out of line.
The thought behind my remarks at this time is that in our negotiations with Japan we are negotiating on the basis of figures that do not do justice to this country. If the valuation of imports from Japan was brought up to where it should be the Department of Trade and Commerce would be in a much better bargaining position because it seems to be a fact today that in order to sell more of our wheat we have to purchase more goods. If these figures were Corrected I believe it would put the minister in a much better position


when he sits down at the bargaining table to negotiate with the Japanese government.
Now that a Canadian team has gone to Europe to take part in the GATT negotiations I should like to point out to the minister that this is a very important matter to the riding I represent because we have a large number of secondary industries which are suffering considerably at the present time. When these negotiations are being conducted I hope the interests of our secondary industries will be taken into consideration most seriously because there is no use closing our eyes to the facts. We have seen the textile industry almost disappear. The small tool and hardware industry is also going by the boards and unless something is done at this time I think conditions will gradually get worse.
I agree with what some hon. members have said in connection with the GATT agreements. I sent to the United States and got the books that were mentioned as costing something like 30 cents each. To me they all prove that the United States is going into the GATT agreements on a much better footing than we are because in our case it seems that the whole matter of negotiation is left to civil servants. It would seem that it is going to be a matter of taking a little bit off here and a little bit off there and our manufacturers do not know what is going to happen. They do not know whether they are going to lose or whether they are going to gain. I hope the Minister of Trade and Comerce will take that into consideration and try to bring about a better deal under GATT than we have had in the past.

Mr. Chairman, I had no intention of taking part in this debate, but seeing the unfair competition to which the graphic arts industries are now subjected by some foreign countries, I felt it my duty to call the attention of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill) to the causes of the present difficulties of the graphic arts industries in Canada.
(Text) :
At the present time the Canadian graphic arts industries are going through a great period of depression. They are facing the greatest competition imaginable from foreign countries. On June 21, 1960 the Minister of Trade and Commerce received a letter from the graphic arts industries association which called his attention to a circular letter issued in Washington informing the United States printing and publishing industry of that country's intention to seek tariff concessions from other countries, including Canada. On June 8, 1960 Mr. David Maclellan, general manager of E.P.A. and of the graphic arts industries

association, a national body embracing all employing printers' organizations from coast to coast, gave an address to the employing printers' association of Montreal entitled "Printing-Canada's Biggest Employer in Manufacturing".
The Canadian graphic arts industries association is a national body embracing all employing printers' organizations from coast to coast, and I have taken most of my information from this brief and from this address. Our small population supports the greatest volume of imported printing of any country in the world. Sixty per cent of United States printing imports are absorbed by Canada and only 5 per cent of our printing exports are absorbed by the United States. We absorb 60 per cent of printing exports manufactured by 170 million people and they only absorb 5 per cent of printed material manufactured by 17 million people. A fair illustration of this unfair and unjust trade imbalance in cash and in bulk is the comparison that for every rabbit we ship to the United States we have to purchase 12 elephants. This may seem like an exaggerated comparison, but I firmly believe that that is what is taking place.
On the United States side the lithographers and printers national association reports that they are regularly watching the import quotas on lithographic and printed products from Canada and other countries. I believe it is the intention of the United States authorities to seek further tariff concessions on the following printing products: dictionaries and encyclopaedias; catalogues, pamphlets and booklets, geographic maps and charts, including atlases, newspapers, advertising matter, playing cards and playing card sheets, bank notes, bonds, cheques, pictures and tickets.
At the present time the Canadian printing industry is subjected to more foreign competition, largely from the United States, than it can comfortably support and this volume is growing rapidly as the department's statistics will show. This practically uncontrolled flow of printed matter from foreign countries, and principally from the United States as I have said previously, is having a serious effect on the employment situation in Canada. It is the cause of much unemployment. Our small population supports the greatest volume of imported printing of any country in the world. Our newsstands, bookstores and postal channels are flooded with foreign printed matter on an unprecedented scale.
Does the minister know that Japan, with printing costs almost half those in the United States and Canada, is preparing to invade the Canadian market and this at a time when
Supply-Trade and Commerce our newsstands, bookstores and postal channels are flooded with printed matter on an unprecedented scale, as I have said previously. The printing industry is the largest employer among manufacturing industries in Canada. This department should be most particularly concerned with the preservation and development of business and industry. It should be interested in the employment situation in Canada. I have here a few excerpts and figures from an address by Mr. David Maclellan, before a printing group on June 8, 1960, one of which is as follows:
The printing industry now spends about $400 million in wages and salaries, about $500 million a year on materials and outside services, as well as something like $65 million a year on machinery, equipment, building construction and repairs, etc.
If a magician removed all the printing from labels and packages in our grocery stores, the food industry and our women too would be at a total loss. A naked package tells you nothing and offers no temptations.
I believe the minister should give serious consideration to the fate of the graphic arts industry in Canada, an industry that is responsible for an expenditure of approximately $1 billion a year and on which depends the livelihood, directly or indirectly, of approximately one million persons. The graphic arts industry, if it is to be correctly understood and appreciated in the nation's economy, can only be accurately described as the first and most indispensable manufacturing industry in Canada. It is a most competitive industry. This may be unfortunate in some ways, but it is a great thing for the country. The graphic arts are first among Canadian manufacturing industries in employment and fourth in dollar value of production. The graphic arts industry employs more creative people and more skilled craftsmen than any other Canadian industry; pays the highest wages of any non-seasonal manufacturing industry and provides the most favourable working conditions.
I should like to talk about the 20 per cent tax placed on United States magazines by the previous government and removed by this government. I know I would be out of order in doing so, so I will not insist. However, I believe I can say that as a result of undue competition from United States publications four national Canadian periodicals were forced out of business in the last 10 years. Dozens of others have had to reduce their frequency of publication or otherwise curtail their usefulness. In 1951 Canadian national periodicals had attained a total combined circulation of 42 million copies per year, while the circulation of United States periodicals was more than 86 million. In 1957 the circulation of Canadian magazines had reached 45.6 million and the circulation of United States magazines in Canada 154

Supply-Trade and Commerce million. I do not know how the circulation figures compare in 1960, now that the tax on United States magazines has been repealed. For the first quarter of 1960 I believe more than 43 per cent of all dollars spent on advertising in Canadian magazines was being spent in two United States magazines. It is a most unfair competition, and I am wondering how the unemployed feel about this favouritism which in a large measure is the cause of a good part of the unemployment situation in Canada.

Mr. Chairman, I welcome this opportunity to say a few words on the estimates of the Department of Trade and Commerce. Very good speeches have been delivered on this subject. I was particularly interested in the speech delivered by the hon. member for Jasper-Edson. Although he is by profession a doctor of medicine, he has a tremendous knowledge of the agricultural industry; particularly on the subject of rape-seed, which he so eloquently described in his speech. It is not my intention to be repetitious and cover the same ground regarding the question of rapeseed. But I would like to add some information to that which has been put on the record, information which has not yet been given.
The western rapeseed producer has done a tremendous job. As one example, this year he has taken one million acres out of the production of wheat and has planted it with rapeseed. These one million acres of rapeseed made a saving to this country, because the Department of Trade and Commerce does not need to worry about how it is going to sell 35 million bushels of wheat; also the treasury does not need to pay storage charges on 35 million bushels which amount to somewhere between 10 and 16 cents per bushel, depending on the year and the amount of grain in storage.
However, there is one thing about this grain that causes great concern to the western rapeseed producer, and that is the freight charge. You are all aware that at the present time, due to the fact that it does not come under the statutory Crowsnest pass freight rate, the producer has to pay 80 cents per hundredweight on rapeseed, while for other grain like wheat, oats, rye and flax the statutory rate is approximately 23J cents per hundredweight. This all came about under the previous government. During their tenure of office they increased the freight rate by something like 150 per cent. Although it may be said that nothing has been done at the present time, let me put this on the record.
Had we followed the same policy that was adopted by the previous government when it allowed freight charges to go up we would


not be paying only 80 cents today for rape-seed, we would be paying $1.20 per hundredweight for it. However, the Canadian producer must pay approximately $5 per acre more in freight charges than if he planted and produced wheat, oats or barley. We produce approximately 1,000 pounds per acre, and since a farmer's average crop is approximately 100 acres, at that rate of $5 per acre he is forced to subsidize the Canadian railroads to the extent of approximately $500 a year. This amounts to approximately $5 million, and I would like to stress this point very much; that the Canadian railroads are filling their coffers with these $5 million per year at the expense of the western rapeseed producers.
But that is not the only thing that is of great concern to us. We hear so much lately about the Russian deal that was made, and how we would be able to sell $2 worth of wheat for every dollar's worth that Russia would buy. But if we had a chance to sell our rapeseed crop every year at a reasonable price we would be able to take out, not only one million acres a year, we would be able to plant about two million or three million acres of rapeseed.
The information that I have is that there is a market available in the world for rape-seed, and this year the prospects are that we will be able to sell at least two thirds of our rapeseed production. Of course we do not know what price we will be getting. However, we expect that it is not going to be down to the same price that we received in 1958. Consequently, the production of this valuable grain went down approximately 200,000 acres a year.
It was mentioned that the export potential of this grain is very promising. But there is another thing that we must be concerned with, and that is supplying the local market with edible oilseeds. At the present time many of the oil-bearing seeds come in from the United States duty free. This came about when a few years ago Canada entered into an agreement with the United States under GATT to allow oil-bearing seeds to come into this country duty free. Of course, it must be said that at that time and perhaps even since then there was a shortage of edible oilseeds in this country But this agreement has outlived its usefulness and must be changed.
I understand there is going to be a delegation from Canada attending the conference of Geneva to take part in the revision of the GATT agreement. I would like to stress this point and bring it to the attention of the minister. I would ask the minister to make efforts to see that the GATT agreement with the United States is changed because, as I said, there are great possibilities for planting

rapeseed in this country; not only for the export market, but also for the local market.
In 1959 nine tenths of the oil that went into the production of products requiring edible oil was imported from the United States and only one tenth was oil obtained from Canadian seed. This has been brought to the attention of the minister through other departments, by myself and other members from the west and particularly, as I mentioned earlier in my speech, by the hon. member for Jasper-Edson. If serious and immediate attention were given to this matter I am sure that in the future the rapeseed producer in the west will do a very valuable job as far as reducing the wheat surplus is concerned and producing grain that has every chance in the world of being a cash product.

Mr. Chairman, Canadians live by foreign trade. Since approximately one quarter of our jobs depend on foreign trade, it is obvious that trade policies must affect every Canadian. My own province of Newfoundland is perhaps more sensitive to trade policies than any other part of Canada, because we export everything that we produce, while everything that we consume has to be brought into the province from outside. Our trading position in the foreign markets is a matter of concern to all of us. We seem to have got ourselves into a position where we are damned if we do, and we are damned if we don't.
Less protection than we have now will affect local manufacturers and, they claim, will increase and aggravate our unemployment problem, which is already a very serious one. On the other hand, more protection will affect our exporters and make it difficult for them to export and will raise the possibility of retaliation in our traditional markets. That too will cause unemployment. So there seems to be no way of avoiding unemployment in either of these courses.
I do not think there is much point in looking for a scapegoat for this situation or in trying to fix the blame. Certainly to whatever extent the government has pursued unwise or wrong policies and to the extent that they have done things they should not have done or have left undone things which they ought to have done they must bear the blame. But it seems to me that a large part of the problem arises from the exercise by a free people of a free choice in their purchases both in the domestic and foreign markets. No government can interfere with the exercise of that free choice without taking sides either against the interests of the consumer or against the interests of the manufacturer.
So there is no easy solution to this problem. I think we must use common sense and be prepared to make painful decisions if they
Supply-Trade and Commerce are necessary. We should not shrink from our duty in that regard. I think we must somehow come to some decision as to what industries in our country are essential and either provide subsidies or find some means of allowing these industries to continue in existence. If other industries are less essential and not in the interests of the economy as a whole, I think we ought not to permit them to exist by increasing tariff protection. That will involve very painful decisions, but I think they are decisions we must face.
Besides this there are a number of avenues which might be explored and one very obvious avenue is to increase our population. I think we have been far too timid in our immigration policies and have lost sight of the fact that the more people we have in Canada the bigger will be our domestic market. And the domestic market is the best market for Canada because it is the only market we can control. When we consider that last year $4.25 billion worth of manufactured goods were brought into Canada we see how important this domestic market is. At the same time the fact that that huge sum of money was spent by Canadians on foreign goods should be a challenge to our manufacturers and one which they should meet without taking the line of least resistance and running to the government for protection whenever the going gets a bit rough.
A second avenue of approach would be to overhaul and improve our long term trading machinery. This involves long term credits and export insurance. There are many places where Canadian goods can compete in foreign markets, yet we lose out to other competitors who do not have a better price but who do have a better credit arrangement which is more suitable to the countries who need and purchase goods which we could otherwise supply.
Another place where I think we have fallen down very badly is in the matter of technical assistance. Here in Canada we have hardly developed enough technologists to supply our own needs, but Canada should be able to export technologists and be in a position to give technical aid and assistance to all these new countries which are coming into existence as well as to other countries which have a potential for becoming our customers. These countries I think we should help with foreign aid and technical assistance to the greatest possible extent.
One very obvious country to which this technical aid and assistance should be given is the British West Indies and the Caribbean countries which are right on our doorstep. Anything we can do to strengthen their economy will put them in a position to become a better market for Canada, and the

Supply-Trade and Commerce kind of friendly relationship we set up in doing that will stand us in good stead.
Nigeria is another country, a young country of 50 million people newly emerging and one of the countries of Africa which does have a stable government. We are losing out in Nigeria, I think, because Nigeria could become a consumer of Canadian flour. But our competitors in the United States have put up flour mills in Nigeria and they are using United States wheat to supply that market. Certainly Canada could have done and should have done the same thing long ago.
Brazil, Spain, and Portugal are three countries of special interest to my province because when Newfoundland was an independent country paddling her own canoe and looking after her own affairs these three countries were our traditional markets. We imported from them salt, oranges, wines and a number of other goods which we do not get now, and they were products of a much superior quality than those we get from our neighbour to the south.
Spain and Portugal are important to Newfoundland because they fish in our waters and produce fish which compete with us. But we are unable to compete with them because the subsidies which they get from their governments together with their low standards of living put them in the position where they can come all the way across the Atlantic and produce fish more cheaply than we can when this fish is right on our own doorstep. These people in Spain and Portugal are not satisfied with their standards of living. They want a better standard of living the same as we do, and I think Canada should make inquiries to see what we can do to help them achieve that. Certainly when their standards of living go up it will put us in a better competitive position with regard to our fish. Therefore let us get together with these countries and find out what technical aid and assistance we can give them and find out what other things we might do to help them strengthen their economy.
Spain and Italy have always been prime markets for salt cod, and to meet that market we have developed special cures of fish called the Spanish cure and the Italian cure. While exports of that quality of fish went up by 8 per cent last year, they are declining now and we are gravely concerned in Newfoundland as to what effect the common market tariffs will have upon our fish exports to those countries. We are all glad that these tariff averages have been deferred until January 1 but the time is going to come when we will have to face that problem, and we do hope


that the minister and his department will do everything possible to see that our fish will not be prohibited from entering that market.
While the Spanish and Italian cured fish exports have come down, the West Indies cured fish exports have gone up. That could result, if we had a normal catch, in a flooding of that particular market with a corresponding reduction in price. I would ask the minister again to consider the placing of a premium on Spanish and Italian grade fish to ensure an increase in the production of that particular variety which is a special kind of light salted fish as compared with the heavy salted fish which is sold the West Indies. It is more profitable today for fishermen to salt their fish heavily because the more salt they use the more rebate they receive, and this offsets the extra trouble they must take to produce Spanish and Italian grades.
Before I sit down I want to say that we should do everything possible to maintain and increase our trade with Japan, not only because this is an important market for Canadian wheat and other products but also because Japan is the one bastion of democracy in Asia, and if that bastion were to disappear, Asia would likely disappear with it. If China-the manpower of China-could be combined with the industrial potential of Japan a most serious position would arise, and that is one of the main objectives of communist strategy in Asia.
What about the Philippines and Formosa?

The Philippines, certainly, but they do not have the same importance to communist strategy, because they are not the industrial nation that Japan is. Japan has to trade with somebody, either with the free world or with communist China. That is why the Kremlin is taking every possible means of trying to force Japan to trade with China and other communist countries. This is the worst thing that could happen for democracy, and we must bear this firmly in mind when we negotiate trade treaties with Japan.

Before this vote is carried 1 should like to say a few words because of the importance of this subject of our foreign trade and domestic policy in the contexl of the minister's statement last evening. Thai statement, as has been pointed out by a good many speakers, was a very optimistic and rosy one, much more optimistic than statements we have received from other sources on our economic situation. If one compares the minister's statement last evening with certain other observations, for instance, on the part of the governor of the Bank of

Canada, he might be pardoned for thinking that we were speaking of different worlds of different Canadas.
The discussion this afternoon has ranged far and wide over the whole area of foreign trade, and that is understandable because of the importance of this subject to our economy. It is true there have been some encouraging developments in the early part of this year in the foreign trade picture as far as Canada is concerned. Our exports have gone up, and our imports have gone up. However, the improvement that is obvious from the earlier figures received a set-back in June which we all hope is only a reflection of a temporary decrease in our trade but which does underline the vulnerability of that foreign trade to world conditions and which emphasizes some of the dangers that face us at the present time.
Our vulnerability is largely, perhaps, in relation to that country with respect to which our trade is most important, that is, the United States of America. The objective of the government to divert a huge proportion of our trade from the United States to the United Kingdom has not been realized, and we remain dependent to an excessive degree on our trade with our neighbour. If there was a pause in the economic development of that country-and there are some indications of that at the present time-this would reflect itself at once in our economic situation. There are trends and developments in the United States at the present time which must give us some cause for anxiety- efforts to put obstacles in the way of our exports into that country, especially in the field of base metals. We should not forget that while our sales of base metals have gone up generally, there is one commodity, uranium, which bids fair to be reduced to practically nothing in the next few years even though at the present time it represents exports valued at $300 million.
Then there is the competition which we are experiencing from the United States in the disposal of our agricultural products, competition which is becoming increasingly difficult as the United States adopts measures to subsidize her agricultural exports in world markets. The effect of this is seen when we realize that while world trade in wheat has gone up over the last year or so, our proportion of that trade has gone down.
Then there is another thing which is quite rightly causing concern with regard to our position in world markets and that is our increasing costs of production. The minister had something to say about this last night when he was talking about Canada's position in a multilateral trading system. Since the end of the second world war that has been
Supply-Trade and Commerce our objective, to bring about a multilateral trading system in the world in which our position would be strong. That has been the important objective to achieve. The minister, speaking about this subject last night, had this to say:
The advent of this multilateral system and the realization of the advantages which might reasonably be expected from it was for many years frustrated by the prevalence of foreign exchange difficulties in many parts of the world. More recently, with the improvement in the world economy and financial conditions, the import controls which had been maintained by many other countries against our goods have been rapidly disappearing. That, of course, is something which we all welcome. As a result, Canadian exporters are for the first time since the war in a position to compete on equal terms in most markets with other most favoured nation suppliers.
In one sense that is no doubt true. They are in a position to compete on equal terms in the sense that the special obstacles in the way of their imports into these countries have been removed. Whether or not they will be in a position to compete on equal terms in other respects will depend on how we can maintain our competitive position in those markets by keeping our own cost of production down.
In any event, as the minister pointed out, the multilateral principle remains the basis of our world trading policy but that principle is under pressure these days. Some of those pressures are pretty obvious. That is one reason why the current and prospective GATT discussions at Geneva are going to be so very important at this time. The pressures I talked about on the multilateral trading system may come-indeed they have already come-from the development of these regional groupings concerning which more than one speaker in this debate has spoken; regional groupings and regional developments for trading purposes not only in Europe but in the western hemisphere.
The Paris meeting of a couple of weeks ago which was attended by my hon. friend the Minister of Finance was important in this connection because it represented another attempt-and I know the government has been continuing this effort over many months- to bring about a reconciliation of these European developments which are so important politically and economically and the multilateral principle which remains the basis of our world trading policy. We should support a move to bring about a reconciliation of that development with the interests of our own multilateral policy by assuring two things, that there will be an association of the United States and Canada with European developments and by doing our best to ensure that these developments will be on a general expansionist rather than restrictionist basis.

Supply-Trade and Commerce It was pointed out by my friend the hon. member for Ottawa West that the United States has taken a more active part in recent months in the effort to associate North America-the United States and Canada- with these developments. We can only hope that this new organization developing out of O.E.E.C. and on a broader basis than O.E.E.C. will do something in both the directions I mentioned, in making an Atlantic area rather than a European area the trading basis and in ensuring that if that is not done the European developments will not hurt our own exports any more than is absolutely necessary.
It is quite true that there are great difficulties in the way of the two European groupings coming together, the common market and the European free trade area but I know the government will have more information about this than is at my disposal. Some of these difficulties in recent weeks have begun to disappear and some progress has been made in the direction of the entry into the common market of the nations of the free trade area.
I studied, as no doubt the minister did, the debate in the British house of commons the other day on this subject. It seems to me that that debate while it did emphasize the difficulties in the way of British association with the common market, especially those difficulties which were derived from her commonwealth position, nevertheless there was a general feeling among members of all parties during the debate that those difficulties were now not so great that they could not be overcome.
There is an article on this subject in the July 30 issue of The Economist which perhaps members of the government concerned with these matters may have read. It underlines the feeling I got from reading the debate myself. Perhaps I may be permitted to quote one or two sentences from the article which is entitled "Honest Doubt". The article quotes Mr. Denis Healey, a leading member of the labour party, as saying toward the end of the debate:
-there is no longer anybody in this house who believes it inconceivable that we should join the common market.
The editorial went on to say:
The case for joining the six-
That is, the common market:
-was strong-and some of the objections of two or three years ago "are less strong now than they seemed then."
That was referring to the remarks of Mr. Harold Wilson. Mr. Selwyn Lloyd who is now the chancellor of the exchequer in winding up this debate for the government, while 

he trotted out all the traditional and conventional arguments against association, according to The Economist said:
-when these phrases were added up they amount to a refusal to be rushed, not much more.
The editorial went on to say, and this I think sums up the present position, that in a matter of such great importance to the United Kingdom only the government could take the decision to move. In the words of the editorial:
Only the government can take the decision to move, and though it is edging closer it has still not been able to make up its mind. The commons did, however, make clear enough that, if and when the government does take the plunge, it will have no difficulty in carrying the house with it.
That is a very important conclusion to be reached by a magazine of such importance as The Economist based on a debate of this kind in the British house of commons. Therefore it becomes of the very greatest possible importance for the government to continue in the efforts it is making to ensure that if this development occurs it is not at our expense. When I say that I do not think that that need necessarily happen because while this European association-the two regional groupings that might get together-would of course mean an adjustment in our trade policies it might be the bind of adjustment by which we would gain freer access into a large trading area, indeed more than we would lose by our preferential position inside the United Kingdom. In any event I know that is the attitude the government has taken in the past. The situation was referred to last night by the minister when he said with respect to these European groupings:
These groupings can develop in ways which will promise larger markets for Canadian goods-
That is the optimistic side of the question:
-or, if they take a restrictive turn, our interests could be prejudiced. Our efforts are being directed to ensuring, so far as possible, that outward looking policies will be pursued which will allow us to continue the mutually advantageous trade relationships which have been developed up to this time.
We on this side wish the government well in any efforts it can take to ensure that this development takes place in Europe in that way, I repeat, however, what I have said so often in this chamber, that this European development will not be enough unless it eventually leads to something wider and deeper both politically and economically and that is the development of an Atlantic freer trade area.
Perhaps in this connection I might put on the record some very wise words of a man who was prime minister of Belgium not so many years ago and who was a great figure in European economic and trade matters. I

refer to Mr. Paul Van Zealand and the words he used when reporting on the Atlantic congress in London. He said this:
These were some of the conclusions of the Atlantic congress. As you notice, every one of these observations leads to the same conclusion: that, in order to meet the actual requirements of the western world, the western world must solve its internal differences, use its imagination and form that economic Atlantic community which, to my mind, is the solution of our problems. It is the solution which will enable Europe at least to eliminate the differences between the common market and the free trade zone. It is the solution which will allow us to help the underdeveloped countries to help themselves, and finally, to achieve a better standard of living.
So much for the foreign trade situation, Mr. Chairman, and I know it has been a very cursory survey. The minister also had something to say about our domestic economic conditions, and he was again very rosy and optimistic on that subject. He said, as found on page 7671 of Hansard:
During the past year economic activity in Canada has moved upward in line with expansionary conditions in the world at large. Canada's gross national product is running appreciably above the level of a year ago.
I doubt very much whether the figures, trends and indices of the last month or two would justify that optimistic conclusion. Applying this expansionary trend to the employment situation, the minister had this to say:
Total employment in June and in the first six months of the current year was approximately 2 per cent above the corresponding period of 1959.
That, of course, is factually true but actually most misleading in terms of reflecting the situation that we face because, as we know and as has been put on the record so many times, while our employment has gone up-of course it has gone up; our population is going up-the fact is that over the period about which the minister is talking the number of new jobs created in this country did not equal the number of people coming into the labour force. It does not matter if we have an employment picture which shows a 2 per cent increase over the corresponding period of 1959 if we have a labour force which represents a greater increase than that over the same period because unless the one is above the other we are going to have unemployment. Therefore that particular statistic does not give me nearly as much comfort as it apparently gives to the minister.
The minister went on to give some other indications of what he considered to be these expansionist tendencies in our economy. As I read these in Hansard this morning I also read the monthly business analysis of Beckett Associates issued in August, 1960 and covering July of this year. These are reputable
Supply-Trade and Commerce economic analysts. They have no particular axe to grind. They certainly have no political prejudices in this matter and I should think no economic prejudices. I should like to quote one or two paragraphs from their analysis covering July which give a rather different picture of the situation than that which was given last night by the minister. One paragraph reads as follows:
The decline in the preliminary July figure for industrial common stock prices indicated the sharpest month-to-month drop of the current cycle. The continuing decline in this indicator has now erased all the gains of the past two years. The stock market holds out little prospect for a fall revival in general business.
While I would not wish to base my conclusions on the stock market exclusively, it is one indicator and there are a good many others. I might mention one or two others referred to in this report. Here is another paragraph:
The central measures of Canadian business activity also remained on the downside in the most recent months. May showed three rising, four falling and two unchanged. The scope of contraction is estimated to have remained the same in July.
Here is another paragraph which has a very direct bearing on what the minister said last night about the increase in the gross national product:
Available monthly data for the second quarter indicate the possibility of a decline of gross national product, with the weakness being widespread by sector but modest in magnitude.
Then, the conclusion of the report reads as follows:
As the summer wears on, with below normal temperatures and below normal levels of business activity, the prospects for an early end to the contraction grow dimmer. Significant recoveries among the leading indicators which are, so far, conspicuous by their absence, must appear if Canadian business is not to end the year on a continuing down swing.
I mention these matters because both in the foreign trade field and in our domestic economic picture it is well to have the whole picture and to put it in perspective. I admit, as the minister said last night, that there have been some very encouraging developments in the foreign trade picture, though not in the last months for which we have the figures. I admit that there are elements of great strength in our domestic economy but anyone who studies the picture at this time, who studies the evidence, who studies the trends, must also admit that there are some very dangerous developments in connection with our economy and that all is not rosy in this economic garden.
We hope that the minister's optimistic predictions will be fulfilled. On the basis of the information we have in addition to that which the minister gave, we are worried that it may not be nearly as easy and comfortable
7712	HOUSE OF
Supply-Trade and Commerce a picture as he would have us believe it is from his own statement last night. There are many other matters of detail which we will be discussing when we come to the other items but this seems to be all I need to say now on the general situation.
