speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have
listened with a great deal of interest to those who have participated in the debate so far, and I gather that there is general agreement that conditions are reasonably good within the country and that our trade and commerce position is satisfactory. I did not sense any severe criticism of anything that is going on at the present time. However, the Leader of the Opposition was disturbed and disappointed because I was not gloomy, depressed and forlorn with regard to present conditions. He rejoices in words like "decrease", "decline" and "recession", looks around the corner with foreboding and is fearful of what may happen next month. Perhaps next year he will have some fear. These things bother him.
Nothing bothers me.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
He wants people to be gloomy about the future. I have said nothing in the remarks I have made concerning Canada's foreign trade position or her internal economy that could be described as unusually optimistic or rosy and so on. It was in very restrained prose that I put forward the picture last night, and I am glad to hear from the Leader of the Opposition that he found time to read my speech this morning since he was not present to hear it.
The situation with regard to our foreign trade is good and is based, as I showed, on the statistics, not on any uncertain forecast.
I put before the house the trade statistics and when we are living in a period when our foreign trade is on the increase and when 1960 will likely set a new record over 1959, why then spread gloom or be depressed? I do not see how it is possible for any minister of trade and commerce at any time in Canada's history to adopt an attitude of gloom. The whole nature of the Department of Trade and Commerce is forward looking. It is a department that is based on the growth and expansion of Canada and it takes a worldwide outlook. Consequently, it would be nothing less than stupid for a person representing the Department of Trade and Commerce constantly to be spreading fear about the future when the facts indicate that things are really going well for Canada and going well because we have the resources, the industrial establishments and a vigorous population in this country to continue the development of Canada.
The governor of the Bank of Canada does not think so.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
A great many countries in the world look to this country with a great deal of admiration and some envy because of the fortunate position we occupy based on our location and resources. Therefore, I make no excuses whatever, and hon. members opposite are at liberty to pretend that I am being unusually optimistic. We have good grounds for confidence in Canada and in Canada's future. All the reports that have attempted to look into the future, five years, 10 or 20 years ahead, paint a picture of a developing Canada with great prospects for her people. It is on that basis that the Department of Trade and Commerce carries on its work.
The Leader of the Opposition expressed his usual fears, his usual anxiety, but had little upon which to base it. He talked about the vulnerability of our foreign trade. Of course, foreign trade is vulnerable if the international situation changes, as it can. He is worried about our dependency on our next door neighbour, the United States. This has bothered Canadians, generation after generation. We have been successful over the last three years in reducing that dependency. I gave the figures last night to indicate that in the last three years imports from that country have declined from 74 per cent of our total imports to 67 per cent at the present moment. The Leader of the Opposition talked about world trade in wheat having gone up and our proportion of it having gone down. This is a misconception with which I dealt in March when we had a rather lengthy discussion on the subject of wheat. It is a misconception which I think is in the mind of the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek. 1 will give you the facts and figures dealing with commercial exports.
Let us deal with all exports.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Commercial exports are the wheat sold for cash. During the inter-war years from 1920 to 1939 Canada's percentage of the world trade in commercial wheat exports was 30.2 per cent and rose in 1958 to 35.7 per cent.
What about total exports?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: There has been no decrease with regard to Canada's share of the world market in wheat, the total world wheat trade.
Will my hon. friend permit a question?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
I will just put this on the record and then the hon. member can ask the question. The total world wheat trade has grown from the inter-war years by 439

million bushels. This increase can be more than accounted for by concessional and political sales, primarily by the United States and Russia. The world commercial export markets for wheat have shown a slight decrease during the same period. Canadian commercial markets have increased from 30.2 per cent to at least 35.7 per cent of the total commercial world exports from the interwar years to 1958. This indicates that Canada continues to be a world leader in wheat sold for cash. Does the hon. member have a question now?
I wanted to ask the minister if he had the figures for the total exports of wheat.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: The total exports of wheat?
Yes, the minister gave them to us as they pertained to commercial sales of wheat, and I wondered if he had them for total sales.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I was pointing out that the figures that are quoted in connection with world trade very frequently indicate commercial sales plus government programs for gifts or subsidies. In so far as the United States is concerned, although in this last crop year their trade in wheat was much larger than ours, over 70 per cent of it was in the nature of gifts,-
That is still competition.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: -whereas our trade in wheat has been chiefly for cash.

I was not arguing that point. I was wondering if the minister had comparative figures available because it seems to me that United States disposal of wheat, plus their sales through usual commercial channels, presents something in the nature of a problem for us. If the minister had these figures available to put alongside the ones he has given it would perhaps help us to appreciate that problem and take the appropriate steps that may have to be taken over the years to help to meet it.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Those figures will be produced in a few minutes by the officials. The Leader of the Opposition, I think, suggested that there was a problem, as did the hon. member for Ottawa West, in the competition we were facing as a result of the United States agricultural disposal program. It is only if these agricultural exports that are given away or given under a subsidized program interfere with the markets that Canada has occupied in the past or might have some thought of occupying in the future that there is any difficulty. At the present time there is very little interference from United
Supply-Trade and Commerce States disposal operations in wheat with Canada's commercial markets. In fact, when we discovered a few years ago that they were interfering with our markets in Europe with barter proposals we asked them to withdraw those proposals and they did. They have not resumed them. Their very large gifts of wheat to India and the other countries of Asia, which are not normal commercial markets for Canada, have not interfered with our exports of wheat.
While I am on the wheat problem, I might just indicate what has happened during the last three years. Our exports of wheat during the last three crop years have run as follows: 320.3 million bushels in 1957-58; 249.1 million bushels in 1958-59; and the estimate for 1959-60 is 276.7 million bushels, making an average of the last three years of 297 million bushels compared with the average of the preceding years of 276 million bushels; the 10-year average, that is 1948-49 to 1957-58, 284.4 million bushels and the 30-year average was 252.6 million bushels. During the last three years, therefore, we have made substantial gains in the sales of wheat abroad, despite the competition that has come from other countries. This is a clear indication that the policy of the government, carried out by the wheat board and supported by those who are in the commercial grain trade has been successful. Our exports of wheat over the last three years have increased and make a better showing than the preceding period.
The hon. member for Ottawa West and the hon. member for Port Arthur followed somewhat the same line as that followed by the Leader of the Opposition in attempting to convey the idea that I was being unusually optimistic with regard to our trade picture. I have dealt with that, I hope, to their satisfaction.
There was some discussion of the question of the GATT conference coming up this September, and the suggestion on the part of the hon. member for Ottawa West and the hon. member for Port Arthur that the government was inactive in connection with this matter, while the United States was being much more active. It is the old, old story of suggesting that Canada is not playing its part and that some other country is doing something that is much more impressive. That is not the case at all. There has been just the same activity in Canada on the part of the government, the same interest on the part of business in Canada, as has been shown in the United States. But it has not received the same amount of publicity.
Canadian businessmen have had every opportunity to present their views to the Minister of Finance, the Minister of National
7714	HOUSE OF
Supply-Trade and Commerce Revenue, the Minister of Trade and Commerce and to officials with regard to the changes that they would hope to see made, the concessions that they hoped Canada would be able to get in the tariff conferences that are coming up. Those suggestions have been given very careful attention.
There is precisely the same type of activity going on in this country as in the United States. We are quite prepared to be as active at the GATT conference as any other country. One of the most experienced civil servants in Canada is heading up our delegation to that conference, and with his wealth of experience I am sure that Canadian interests will be adequately protected.
I was not quite sure whether the member for Ottawa West was suggesting that representatives of business should have an offiicial position-
No.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: -on the Canadian delegation to Geneva.
No, I was not suggesting that.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: They will have the opportunity of making representations and perhaps being there as observers.

Mr. Chairman, perhaps before the minister leaves that point I could ask him this question. That was the very thing I wanted to find out; what arrangements had been made by the government in that respect; what arrangements, if any, had been made for the government team to receive representations in the various cities of Canada, and that sort of thing.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
The information given to us just the other day by Hector McKinnon was that he has received scores of delegations and representations from businessmen right across the country.
Then at the same time during the course of the negotiations-which will be prolonged, as the hon. member for Ottawa West knows, and will extend over several months-there will be opportunities for Canadian businessmen to make further representations.

Mr. Chairman, on this point I would like permission to ask the minister another question. He will recall the debate during this session about the disclosure of a big trading nation, the United States, as to the items upon which they would propose to negotiate with the fellow partners in Canada at a fall conference.
I wonder, in view of the remarks of the hon. member for Ottawa West this afternoon, whether the minister would explain Canada's policy which seems to refrain from indicating


to the industries of this country and to our trading partners in advance our possible levels of trading negotiation that we have in mind prior to the actual assembling of the conference.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am not sure that the hon. member's statement can be answered completely, or whether he is being quite realistic about the situation. A preliminary list of matters that the United States government is going to take up-may propose to take up-at the conference at Geneva was published. It was a published document, available to the public anywhere. Business in the United States made its representations with regard to that. As was pointed out earlier this afternoon, a final list will be prepared secretly, by the United States and will form the basis for their negotiating team when they deal with the other countries at Geneva.
Canadian businessmen have full knowledge of Canada's position. They know what is the present tariff. They know what the concessions have been in the past at Geneva. They know what the tariff is with regard to other countries, our trading partners. There is nothing that is not available to Canadian business in Canada, from the standpoint of information pertaining to these matters. On the basis of that they have made their representations to us.
The question was raised by some hon. members as to what concessions could Canada get; what had Canada to bargain with at the conference table at Geneva. All that information is in the hands of our efficient team that will be in attendance at Geneva. The documents setting out the obligations of Canada and other countries under GATT are available. It is on that basis that these negotiations will be carried on.
The United States has, under authority, an opportunity to make certain reductions. In return the United States will be asking for certain concessions. Canada is in a somewhat similar position. It is a bargaining counter at which people give and expect to get something in return, and we have our protection under GATT with regard to the contractual relations that countries have entered into there. If changes are made in those arrangements, then something must be given in return; or a country that thinks it is being harmed will ask for something in return. This leads on to the other discussion concerning European region groupings and the possibility of the United Kingdom-

Mr. Chairman, before the minister comes to that point would he perhaps be a little clearer in defining the difference between the policy of the United States government, a member of GATT, and

the Canadian government, a member of GATT, in announcing in advance the commodities that it would prefer to have as important trading items at one of these major conferences.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I mentioned the fact that this was a preliminary list which they made public. They are not disclosing the final list. There is a difference between the two types of government in the United States and Canada. Under their law they make their start in the way they have done. That is not the custom in Canada. But at the same time, under our system the information is available for Canadian business and Canadian businessmen have been here interviewing ministers and interviewing the delegation that will be in attendance at Geneva. So there is just a difference that arises because of different laws and different types of government. But the objective is the same in the end.

Mr. Chairman, because of the importance of this September conference of GATT I thought perhaps the minister might want to let parliament know what was in the minds of the Canadian delegation as major items of perhaps substantial change, such as has been indicated publicly by the United States government.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: We are going to the table to negotiate, and you do not disclose everything you are going to do to the people who are also going to sit at that table with you. Nor has the United States disclosed these things. They have put out feelers as to what they might like to happen and have suggested this and suggested that. But that is quite different from what will occur when they finally end up at the conference table in Geneva and start to bargain with other countries that will be represented there.

I appreciate the minister's comment but on the other hand we have all had experience with the fact that we have references to the tariff board. In connection with some of the items in the tariff schedule they are inevitably tied up with GATT agreements, so it is quite obvious that if our tariff board under our processes has recommendations to make, some of these items in the tariff schedule are going to be of important concern to Canada at this unusually important GATT conference.
Having regard to that I thought the Minister of Trade and Commerce might review some of the items about which there is a suggestion from the tariff board that we should have an upward or a downward reduction in our tariff arrangements which would 79951-0-487
Supply-Trade and Commerce be prominent in our presentation of negotiations at the GATT conference this fall.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
The hon. member for
Kenora-Rainy River is well versed in these matters and he will recall that in the course of the budget speech reference was made to some of the tariff matters on which negotiations might be carried on. He is also well aware that matters which are before the tariff board will not immediately be up for negotiation, and he has stated his knowledge of the contractual obligations which Canada and other countries associated with Canada have under the GATT agreement. He is not surely expecting some announcement here with regard to a detailed list of subjects. This is in the hands of the negotiating team and will be left to them and to their discretion; and they have been very discreet in the past, because this is the delegation which was at the previous GATT conference dealing with tariff items.

Before we leave that point may I ask just one more question. The United States government published a list of the products on which it might consider offering tariff concessions for the purpose of obtaining from other countries tariff concessions to the benefit of United States export trade. It is clear that the list was merely a preliminary one and was designed to provide an opportunity for all persons in the United States interested to submit any information they might have on whether or not the United States government should offer concessions on individual products.
Now, my question is this. Did the Canadian government submit any such preliminary list to Canadian industry or did it otherwise publish any other list so that Canadian industry could after seeing that preliminary list make representations to the government as to what the industry thought the government should do?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
The United States action was taken under their law because they are obliged to put out a preliminary list. We are not required so to do, but every opportunity was given to Canadian industry and they were so advised by letter and by advertisement to make representations to the government with regard to matters which concern them and which would be perhaps the subject of discussion at the tariff conferences. The hon. member for Ottawa West has been through this before, and was he not parliamentary secretary at the time the earlier negotiations were held? We are following exactly the same practice as in the past. There were no suggestions in those days that lists should be widely published and our law does not so require.

Supply-Trade and Commerce

There was pretty intensive preparation in those days and what I am worried about is to make sure that there has been sufficient intensive preparation. I have nothing but praise for the head of the government team who will be conducting the negotiations, but I am wondering whether or not the government has done enough by way of making preparations.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I will immediately allay the fears of the hon. member for Ottawa West. The most intensive preparation has been made for the conference, and it is just a few days ago that the Minister of Finance and myself discussed most of the problems with the negotiating team. We are quite satisfied that they go there fully prepared and that they have heard from all segments Canadian industry who are interested in the matter. The way is still open for others who may wish to make further representations, but the most intensive preparation has gone into the preparation for the conference.

May I ask a question in this connection. I appreciate fully, as the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River does, that full disclosure of the specific commodity objects that the government has in mind would be unwise during this stage of negotiation. But the Minister of Agriculture during this session has on a number of occasions indicated with regard to certain agricultural imports that an opportunity would be seized by the government at the September meeting to permit freer action on the part of the government with regard to the importation of agricultural products, particularly those from the United States.
Is the minister in a position to indicate whether the Minister of Agriculture spoke out of turn, or what has the government in mind?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: The Minister of Agriculture does not speak out of turn. It is a practice which is well known to the hon. member for Essex East. He speaks with knowledge and at the proper time, and if this question is of great importance to the hon. member for Essex East he will have an opportunity of asking the Minister of Agriculture that question on orders of the day when we next meet.

That is hardly a satisfactory answer. I must say I admire the minister in seeking to defend his colleague and the indiscretions of his colleague, if that is what they are, but I imagine that the conduct of the negotiations is under the Minister of Trade and Commerce. Am I right in that or is that one of the pre-emptive rights of the Minister of Finance who seeks to cover the whole ambit of government? I take it


the Minister of Trade and Commerce is sitting next to the Minister of Finance, and as I suspect the Minister of Agriculture would not have part in those negotiations, this is the moment when the Minister of Trade and Commerce should tell me whether the government proposes to be relieved of commitments now which in any way restrict action with regard to the importation of agricultural commodities from the United States which seem to compete with agricultural production in Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Any of these matters which require negotiation will be taken up at the conference. This problem that the hon. member raises with regard to the Minister of Agriculture we will draw to his attention and see if he has any further representations to make. But I must point out to the hon. member for Essex East that the Minister of Agriculture is entirely discreet. He does not get carried away as does the hon. gentleman opposite.

This is an important matter. The Minister of Agriculture has said in this session on two occasions, that the government was going to take action at the September meeting which would enable it in turn to take action against the importation of agricultural products from the United States into Canada. The government is denied that opportunity now because of action taken by the previous administration.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce cannot be compelled to give an answer, but his refusal to give an answer in the particular context leaves one justified in drawing the conclusion that the Minister of Agriculture was talking out of turn.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Trade and Commerce; Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: Would the hon. member give the reference in Hansard?
I have not got them but if the whip had been in the house at the time, as he sometimes is not, he would know what I was talking about.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
I would like to deal briefly with the remarks made by the hon. member for Port Arthur, but apparently he is not available at the moment so perhaps I should wait until he happens to return.
The hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek made quite an interesting contribution to the debate this afternoon based on a very careful study of conditions and of research work. I think he has placed before the committee some material which is of considerable importance. I think I have already dealt with some of the remarks the hon. member made concerning Canada's share of the world wheat market, and I shall not go further into

that question now. I shall have to suggest to my hon. friend that his criticisms of the activities of the officials of the wheat board would more properly be taken up with the members of the wheat board when they are here in attendance before the agriculture committee of the House of Commons, as they are each session. Officials present at those meetings have an opportunity to make replies and to defend their position. Here in the House of Commons the minister is responsible for the acts of officials, and I certainly accept full responsibility for the acts of the Canadian wheat board. I should like to tell my hon. friend that it is in those terms he should discuss problems here in the House of Commons: let the criticism be directed toward the responsible member of the government who then will deal with the matter.
The Canadian wheat board, as far as I am concerned has acted during the past three years in accordance with the policy of this government, which has been a policy of the expansion of our wheat sales in countries outside Canada, and I have given figures to indicate that success has attended that policy. The wheat board has been very active. I have accompanied members of the wheat board to Europe on three different occasions to confer with importers of Canadian wheat in the United Kingdom, in Belgium, in Holland, West Germany, Switzerland and the Scandinavian countries. The members of the wheat board have toured the Latin American countries, Japan and the Far East. In addition, during the last six months they have been in Africa.
They have been very active in attempting to extend the sale of Canadian wheat and to open up new markets. They appreciate the fact, as we do here, that it is essential to open up new markets for Canadian wheat in Africa if we are to maintain our export position. The hon. member for Burin-Burgeo, I think it was, said we should have been more active with regard to the sale of wheat flour in Nigeria. Well, that country has been visited. I have talked with officials of that country.
Members of the wheat board have visited Nigeria, and a concrete effort was made to establish a Canadian flour mill in that country. Other interests prevailed, but I would remind hon. members that this activity is not solely one which is the responsibility of the wheat board or of the Canadian government. Those who are actively engaged in the flour milling industry or in the purchase and sale of wheat must look afield now to establish further opportunities for the sale of Canadian wheat and flour abroad. The 79951-0-4871
Supply-Trade and Commerce wheat board has been doing what it can to promote such sales, but other segments of the industry must similarly be active. The wheat board as I see it has over the last three years been very active in promoting the sale of Canadian wheat flour. They may have made mistakes here and there, but who does not. I cannot at this moment here in the House of Commons do other than protect those who, because of their absence, cannot reply to criticisms which are made of them.
The constructive suggestions made by the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek will be drawn to the attention of the Canadian wheat board and we shall see whether the changes he suggests can be introduced or if they are adequate to meet conditions. I do not wish to create the impression that I am rejecting the suggestions he has put forward, because they will be examined with the greatest of care. I think he was somewhat mistaken with regard to some alleged losses of sales in certain markets, and I think he is not correct in suggesting that Russia has been capturing new markets at our expense. There was a sale of wheat a year ago to the Netherlands at a time when we did not have sufficient quantities of No. 5 wheat, which was what the millers in the Netherlands required.
The hon. member mentioned France as a market for Canadian wheat. It is very rarely that France is a customer for our wheat. France has been an exporter of wheat for many years and when any wheat is bought we have to find out what kind of wheat is purchased. If it is soft wheat, then we do not supply it. We have sold durum wheat to France, and hope to do so again, but I question if it is accurate to say that Canada has lost out to any other country in such foreign markets as this. If that has happened it is probably because of the type of wheat which was desired by the purchasing country, or it may have been related to price.
We have no control over purchasers. If they should wish on some occasion to purchase wheat from some country other than Canada there is nothing we can do about it. There may be other factors involved, factors of which we have no knowledge; barter arrangements or something like that. I am not at all convinced that Canada has lost out in her normal markets overseas through any unusual competition or greater activity on the part of a country such as Russia. I think the members of the Canadian wheat board and of the grain trade have been very active in selling our wheat abroad and that they have done a very fine job for the western Canadian producer.

Supply-Trade and Commerce

Mr. Chairman, would the minister permit at this point an intervention which I think might be appropriate. On the question of markets, and particularly markets for flour, I wonder if the minister would expand upon the welcome comments he has just made with respect to the matter of our exports to the West Indies and would he relate his remarks to the representations that were made by the western Canada liaison committee this year with respect to competition having relation to subsidies on flour exports to the West Indies market which nave in the past always been very important to Canada?
In so far as our competition with the United States is concerned, would the minister give an up-to-date picture as to whether or not through the wheat board or otherwise we are keeping in keen competition with the pricing opportunities that are available to the West Indies from United States markets.
The minister knows that in my riding we have an important flour milling industry as we have throughout western Canada and in other places. One of the four or five points presented to the government when the wheat pools and others last met the cabinet was that the government and Canada as a whole might possibly be of assistance to the grain producer in meeting subsidy competition in so far as the supply of flour was concerned, particularly into the West Indies market.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the question of our flour exports has been given very careful consideration. I have looked into this on many occasions during the past two or three /ears. I have discussed with the wheat board and representatives of the milling industry and others the problem of the competition suffered from the United States subsidization of their flour exports. That has been met in part by wheat board action in assisting the flour exporters in Canada. The situation at the present moment is that competition is still keen between Canadian flour exporters and United States exporters.
Are we holding our own?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
The over-all picture indicates that we are holding our own but here and there we have suffered a rather serious decline. British Guiana is an example of a place where our flour exports have declined rather markedly but the over-all picture indicates that we are holding our own.
This has been the subject of consultation when we have had meetings with representatives from the United States. We have impressed upon them the importance to us of maintaining our flour markets in areas in which they are also active. It is only about a year and a half ago that representatives of

the Canadian wheat board and the flour milling industry were in the West Indies making a careful survey of the situation there.
I will consult with the wheat board again after this session is over with particular reference to the problem the hon. member has raised because it is just as important to us to maintain our exports of flour as it is to maintain our exports of wheat. In fact, as new countries are developing around the world they seem to become interested in establishing flour mills within their borders. This means a reduction in imports. We are watching that situation very closely and will make this a special point of investigation later this summer.

Will the minister agree that that was one of the four or five points of possible relief as a result of government intervention, mentioned when the western grain growers' representatives came before the cabinet? Was there not a price tag on that? Was it not a relatively small sum, $6 million, perhaps?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I cannot give the hon. member the figure. That type of assistance has been asked for previously. It may have appeared in the brief presented by the group mentioned but it certainly has been raised before and has been the subject of discussion.

Mr. Chairman, the minister has referred to cash sales of wheat. Is it the policy of Canada to make sales on a credit basis? If that is so, what is the reason why we cannot sell some of these countries our wheat on a credit basis? Is it because we cannot carry the load?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
No, Mr. Chairman, we have made sales of wheat on credit. The chief example is Poland to whom we have sold substantial amounts of wheat on credit. Sales of wheat on credit were also made to Israel and India, but the general policy is to sell for cash.
This matter has been talked over on many occasions. We do not consider it advisable to sell wheat or flour on credit to countries that are normally commercial markets for wheat and flour. It is material that is consumed shortly after it is delivered. It is not machinery or something that has a long life ahead of it. Consequently, we have not gone beyond the examples I have given of selling wheat on credit terms nor have we gone as the United States has into the field of accepting foreign currency for wheat which is the same thing as selling it on credit. That is a field we have not entered extensively at all.
We do not see the need for doing this. Two thirds of the wheat we export from

Supply-Trade and Commerce
Canada goes to the United Kingdom and the countries of western Europe and they are cash customers. Our second largest customer is Japan, also a cash customer. With those countries as customers there is no need to sell wheat on credit terms and consequently we have not entered that field and it is not our policy to do so.

On that point, would the minister indicate to the committee whether there have been any defaults on credit contracts? I believe that all these credit contracts have been arranged through the exports credit insurance corporation. Have there been any defaults? The minister mentioned Poland, India and Israel.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: No, there have been no defaults.
What was the maximum term for any one contract?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Three years was the length.
Other hon. members have raised questions which I do not want to gloss over without giving them attention but if I have failed to answer any point perhaps hon. members would raise their questions when the relevant items are before us. At this stage I wish to thank hon. members for their contributions dealing with the general subjects that are open for discussion on the first item.

Mr. Chairman, perhaps the minister may not be disposed to thank me for my additional contribution but I propose to make it in any event because his rather peevish words at the beginning of his statement demand some reply by me and I should not like to disappoint the minister by not producing one.
The trouble with the minister is that he gives us his picture of the economic and trade conditions from carefully selected statistics and when we put forward some other facts and other suggestions which bring the picture into a better focus as we see it the minister then accuses us, and he has done it so many times, of relishing the gloom we are trying to create and all that kind of tawdry talk. If we put forward observations which attempt to correct the false impression, as we see it, created by the minister, we are doing in this house what other people are doing in the country, the governor of the Bank of Canada and other bank presidents, economic analysts, and I have quoted one this afternoon, and businessmen. I do not suppose the minister would accuse them of revelling in gloom or selling the country short or having no faith in Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Would the Leader of the Opposition permit a question?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Will he put forward statistics indicating lower export trade or decreased sales or things of that nature? Let us have the other side of the picture about which he is talking.

I tried to give the other side of the picture in what I thought were very restrained terms, but they were not restrained enough to prevent the minister becoming annoyed. The June figures for export trade are down.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: One month.

The minister has manipulated the statistics about wheat but I will put them on the record to show that they are creating anxiety. The hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek attempted to reflect that anxiety. When we do this the minister says we have no faith in Canada. The minister and some of his colleagues often fall into the habit of identifying Canada with the government. We have no faith in the government. We have great faith in Canada. The trouble with the minister is that we will not move a vote of thanks to him for his operations as cheer leader in the government. We propose to continue as I have done this afternoon, and as we will do on the estimates of the Minister of Finance, to give the picture as we see it and try to get it into balance.
Perhaps the minister might deal with at least one of the statements I made this afternoon. He said last night, and I apologize to the minister for not having had the pleasure of hearing his statement, that Canada's gross national product is running appreciably above the level of a year ago. I quoted from the monthly business analysis of Beckett Associates this paragraph:
Available monthly data for the second quarter indicate the possibility of a decline of gross national product-[DOT]
Who is right? The minister had a good deal to say about wheat. I talked about the proportionate decline of Canada's share of world wheat marketing. That was the expression I used, and the figures show that has in fact happened. I quote from a Canadian Press story based on official statistics because I have not the bureau's figures here. I think the minister will accept these figures. The story reads in part as follows:
Canadian shipments of wheat and wheat flour in terms of wheat declined to 235,900,000 bushels during the first ten months of the current crop year from 243,800,000 in the corresponding period last year. The Canadian share of the international market supplied by the four major exporting countries eased to 29 per cent from 32 a year ago.

Supply-Trade and Commerce
That is all I stated and that seems to be quite accurate. The minister tried to shift the argument by talking about commercial marketings.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: That is what is important.
I was talking about all marketings. Whether marketings by the United States of America are commercial or non-commercial they compete with Canadian marketings in the markets of the world.
It is not marketing; it is a gift.
It is part of the world wheat trade whether it is given away or whether it is sold.
It is a gift.

The effect on the Canadian exporter and the Canadian farmer is exactly the same whether he is competing with wheat given away by the United States or whether he is competing with wheat sold by Argentina.
When you are talking about markets you should talk about markets, not gifts.

Therefore what I said was quite right. I want to ask the minister something else because without success we have tried to get some indication from his department and from the minister as minister of the department about the economic outlook. We tried to get it through seeking the tabling of the report, Canadian Economic Outlook, 1960. It would have been very interesting to have had that report tabled inasmuch as it was tabled in 1959 after having been surreptitiously used in 1958. So the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate asked this question on July 30, as found at page 7266 of Hansard:
In order to assist the committee of supply in considering the unemployment problem, will the Minister of Trade and Commerce table the Canadian Economic Outlook for I960?
The minister replied:
The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate is asking for the tabling of a confidential report, and last evening the hon. member for Essex East said that this was contrary to the usages of parliament. I think perhaps we shall not do it.
In other words, "I think perhaps we shall not table that report", said the minister. When the subject was brought up on Monday, August 1, by way of a motion to table the report, this report which the minister had said the day before could not be tabled because it was confidential, the minister said as found on page 7324 of Hansard:
Mr. Speaker, there is no such document for 1960.
In 24 hours the existence of this document disappeared. Not only was it a document


which could not be tabled, as we were told the day before, but it is now a document which does not exist. I should like to ask the minister if he can recon'cile that rather confusing contradiction and whether he can also tell the committee if there is any report of that nature from the department. Perhaps it might throw some light on the department's views on the economic situation. It may have been given a different title or form. It may not be called, "Canadian Economic Outlook for 1960", but is there an annual report under any other name which deals with the same matter?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: A series of confidential reports from the economics branch is submitted in the Department of Trade and Commerce. So many hon. members on the other side have said that confidential reports should not be tabled that I rather wonder at the Leader of the Opposition asking about the matter now. He is quite aware that confidential reports are passing over the desks of ministers every week.

Mr. Chairman, I do not think the minister can really expect to convince hon. members by this reply. The minister did say in answer to a motion put the other day by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate that there was no economic report in existence. That is the fact but, as the Leader of the Opposition has just indicated, in commenting on my statement, that there were confidential documents which should not be produced, the minister acknowledged that there was in fact such a report in existence. Thus the two replies cannot be reconciled.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I did not say there was such a report.
My hon. friend did. He told the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate that there was no such report. Here is the question of the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: What day was that?

This was on Saturday, July 30, just a week ago today, not so long ago really as to have been forgotten. The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate said as found on page 7266 of Hansard:
In order to assist the committee of supply in considering the unemployment problem, will the Minister of Trade and Commerce table the Canadian Economic Outlook for 1960?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: If I am not mistaken, an order of the house was made with regard to this matter.
There was an order with respect to the volume for 1959, sir. Is the minister going to give an answer?

speakeroldname: Hon. Gordon Churchill (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate is asking for the tabling of a confidential

report, and last evening the hon. member for Essex East said that this was contrary to the usages of parliament. I think perhaps we shall not do it.

Does the minister recall an
exalted precedent?
Let there be no question about it. Our position always has been that confidential documents of that character were matters that were prepared for the members of the government. But that is not the position taken by this government, as we know from the conduct of the Prime Minister with regard to this particular document in the year 1958 when, without any reservation, he divulged it to parliament. What the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate had clearly established was that there was such a document this year. The minister denied it at a later date.
What we want to know from the minister today is-is the economic report in the form used in 1959 and 1958 still in existence? If it is not in existence, in what form does the minister receive from his officials this report? Has the name of the report been changed? Is its circulation now limited to certain members of the cabinet? I would hope that the Minister of Labour would be one of those receiving it. Has it changed its colour? Is its name no longer that of the years previous? In other words, is the minister trying to disguise its characteristics and because it is not in the same form as previous years- although he would still be contradicting himself-saying that there is no longer such a report as was revealed by the Prime Minister? Then, when he is asked by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate about that report, the minister can say, no, there is no such report in 1960.
We want to ascertain whether, if there is not in exactly that form such a report, there is such a document which should be produced according to the precedent which the Prime Minister himself established. If there is, will the minister table it? Will he tell us, if he will not table it, what is the broad outline of it so that we can ascertain the kind of answers which the Leader of the Opposition has been seeking to elicit from the Minister of Trade and Commerce, and the kind of answers which the governor of the Bank of Canada has not hesitated to give to the country. However, the Minister of Trade and Commerce says that is not the kind of reply that should be given by the Minister of Trade and Commerce.
The immediate question now is, is there such a document known as the "Canadian Economic Outlook for 1960"? This is something that has always existed. Perhaps if the minister would give us an unequivocal answer to that, we could get responses which
Supply-Trade and Commerce would reveal whether or not there is an economic outlook available, and presented to the Minister of Trade and Commerce in another form.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: The hon. member for Essex East, on the one hand, states as he did in July that confidential reports should not be tabled. It is contrary to the usages of parliament. The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate said the same thing, and I think the Leader of the Opposition said just about the same thing.
That is our position.
We are talking about your position.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: These hon. members are trying to occupy two positions, as they so frequently do. They place a question on the order paper asking for the tabling of a confidential report.
Which is the policy of the present government.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
It is not the policy of the government whatever, except at the request of hon. members opposite who asked for the tabling of the document which was a year old, and it was tabled after a whole year had elapsed. A second document with a similar title was tabled the following year. Here the other day the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate wanted to have the report for 1959 tabled, and the house refused to grant that request. Then he asked for the "Canadian Economic Outlook for 1960", knowing that he was asking for something which, if it is in existence, is a confidential document according to the definition of hon. members opposite.
Hon. gentlemen opposite cannot have it both ways. You cannot have it confidential and say it should not be disclosed and then, in the next breath, say it is a confidential document which should be disclosed. This is more confusing than the usual state of the opposition. You simply cannot occupy these two positions, nor can the hon. member for Essex East now come forward and ask for full information with regard to confidential reports in a department. He wants to know if there is a confidential report by another name, how many confidential reports come to my office and how many are distributed to the members of the privy council. He wants the whole thing disclosed. He knows, having been a member of the privy council, that would be contrary to the oath.

Is that a question? I fully agree, but the point is this: This government does not take that position. The

Supply-Trade and Commerce Prime Minister revealed this confidential document and said that it should be revealed. Now, having taken that position we are entitled in the following years to ask for it. We did ask for it, and it was tabled. We are asking for it again, because that is the government's attitude with regard to this confidential document. I may tell my hon. friend now that if he wants to pass this general item he should not fail to recognize the logic of this position.
Threats, threats.

Hon. gentlemen say "threats". This is not a threat, it is just an examination of the statement made by the minister. We have always taken the position that confidential documents addressed to the minister should be so considered, but that is not the position that this government has taken in 1958 or in 1959 when they tabled the documents. We are asking, on the basis of the precedents which this government established-and my hon. friend was the instrument in 1959-that the performance be repeated and the "Canadian Economic Outlook for 1960" be tabled.

I wonder if the minister would indicate just how many economists there are in his department today as compared with three years ago. I recall very vividly that the financial critic of the opposition in the budget debate on April 6, 1954 referred very critically to the increase in the size of the staff of economists employed by the government. I do not accept that view. I have no objection to the employment of economists. However, I have objection to the employment of economists if their reports are not advanced and not acted upon. I should like to know just what advance there has been in the Department of Trade and Commerce in the employment of economists.
I have a folder here, which all hon. members can see, containing some of the recent civil service advertisements. There are requests galore for information officers, for economists, for photographers and so on. The point is that this year we have a heavy staff of economists, and apparently the minister does not want to receive their advice and there are no reports from them.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I object to that statement immediately, that I do not want to receive their advice and there is no report made to me. I said just a few minutes ago that reports of the economic branch of our department were sent to me regularly.
Mr. Chairman, the minister on July 30 said, or indicated that there was a report "Canadian Economic Outlook for 1960".

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I said no such thing.
On August 1 he said there was no such report. When was he right ?
He is always right.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: That is an inaccurate statement by the Leader of the Opposition.
You put it on Hansard twice.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I did not put it on Hansard twice. I said no such thing. The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate was asking for a confidential document. In his opinion, that is what it was.

Mr. Chairman, just so the record may be clear, I say this to the minister. On page 7324 of Hansard there appears:
Motion No. 136-Mr. Pickersgill:
For a copy of the "Canadian Economic Outlook for 1960", prepared in the Department of Trade and Commerce.

speakeroldname: Hon. Gordon Churchill (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, there is no such document for 1960.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: That is correct.

What did you say the day
before?
Is that the situation?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: That is the situation.

The day before, the minister said, at page 7266:
The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate is asking for the tabling of a confidential report, and last evening the hon. member for Essex East said that this was contrary to the usages of parliament. I think perhaps we shall not do it.
Which answer is correct?
Both.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: They are both correct. The hon. member for Essex East thoroughly understands the situation.
I certainly do.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate was asking for a confidential document that he considered to be in existence and that he knew he should not be asking for because he had stated-
He got it the year before.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
-that a confidential document could not be tabled, and no matter what was done in the past, no document for 1960, 1959, 1958 or 1957 was made public in the year in which it was produced. Yet despite that he asks for what he considered to be a confidential document. He said that is what he had asked for, and the house understood it perfectly. Then the next day.

contrary to what he had stated should not be done, he puts a question on the order paper asking for the tabling of a report for this year-

It had been on the order paper
for a week.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
-which I said was not in
existence.

Mr. Chairman, the Minister of Trade and Commerce indicates that the opposition gets confused. If there is any confusion to be shown that should raise concern in this committee or in parliament it is the confusion of the minister, as evidenced by his attitude on this day on this subject.
He started oil by stating that the opposition had been asking for these reports and that this was the situation. The facts of the situation are, as he well remembers, that the Prime Minister of	Canada-the	new Prime
Minister of Canada-on January 20, 1958, in the midst of a very dramatic production in the course of a debate in this house quoted excerpts from a document which he waved very dramatically, a white document fastened together with heavy brass tabs and with some blue pieces of paper sticking on the tabs, obviously a blue cover had been torn off, although parts of the cover were still remaining on it.
He quoted excerpts at length. It was obvious from the technique that he used that he was quoting only chosen phrases and quoting them out of their context. I was the one who asked him, after he had carried on this performance for quite some time, to table the document.
There was a great deal of hesitation on that occasion about tabling the document then; he was going to table it later. But he finally did table it at the dinner adjournment, and that document, which I took the precaution of looking at immediately, was rather an interesting one, because parts of the blue cover were still on it, although he said there was no cover on it and he did not know anything about the cover. Be that as it may; I am not discussing that now.
That is the origin and the genesis of this business. The next year, when the opposition asked for the production of the document for the year 1958, the answer given by the Prime Minister was, no, it could not be tabled. That was on June 18 of 1958. The Prime Minister made his position clear, that he would not table it then, that it was too early. But he did not say he would not table it later. I think he indicated-if my recollection is right -that he would table it at the end of the year. On January 16, 1959, a request was made for that document and the Prime Minister I believe indicated that the Minister of Trade 79951-0-488
Supply-Trade and Commerce and Commerce would table it that day. Well, it was tabled on January 16; it was tabled that day.
What day?

January 16, 1959. In the 1960 session there was a request about the publication; there were two requests, and nothing was done. There was no indication that there was an objection to tabling the 1959 document at the end of the year. There was a motion, and when the motion was put on February 15, 1960, it will be noted that there would no longer be any objection to a motion of that type.
The house had to vote on it and the house turned it down. The minister did not say then that there was no such document for 1959. He did not give any reasons, and certainly any earlier objections that there were on the part of the government could not be effective.
Then when the copy of the "Canadian Economic Outlook for 1960" was asked for, the minister took the strange and conflicting position indicated in Hansard of July 30 and again in Hansard of August 1, both of which have been quoted here. I would like to know categorically from the minister: first, was there any such document for the year 1959; and second, was there any such document for the year 1960?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I do not mind answering those questions at all. First let me deal with the so-called confidential document of 1957 about which hon. members of the opposition have been so disturbed. It was called a confidential document. I found the distribution list of that document in 1957, and the same distribution list was used in 1958.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: It was a carelessly treated confidential document because 175 copies were mimeographed. It was very widely distributed; I think over 150 of those were sent out.
Several hundred by the Liberal association.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
I am speaking of the 1957
one. One went to the Canadian National Railways, and a copy to the library at the Royal Military College at Kingston. Yet hon. friends opposite have been telling us for years that this was a confidential document whose contents could not be disclosed and it was improper to bring it to the light of day.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
That was the confidential document spread across this country, with a word on it marking it confidential and that word meaning nothing.

Supply-Trade and Commerce
Meaning nothing to some people.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: The document of 1958 followed the same distribution list. When I investigated it I found and considered that that was quite improper for a confidential document, and the document of 1959 was issued on a restricted list and was kept strictly confidential.
I bet it was.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: No "Canadian Economic Outlook for 1960" such as the one for 1957, 1958 and 1959 has been published.
Why?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Does that answer the question of the hon. member for Ottawa West?

It only answers part of it. In the foreword to the documents tabled in 1958 and 1959 it indicates that the reports contain a regular series of statements on the economic outlook prepared for the use of the federal minister and civil servants concerned. The purpose of the reports is to appraise the influences operating in the economy as they are likely to affect the general level of economic activity in the year. Then it says the present report was completed in March and a supplement containing the usual statistical tables will be made available at a later date.
The estimates show the same number of economists in the branches last year, although the grading has changed slightly. What I want to know now is, does the minister have the benefit of any similar publication for his own use?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I have the benefit of the advice of the economists in the economics branch and that advice is available day after day, week after week and month after month. It is given and it is appreciated.

That is not the question I asked. My question was: Is there any document of a similar nature appraising the influences operating in the economy as they are likely to affect the general level of economic activity for the year prepared now? Does the minister have the benefit of any such document?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
This is getting to be rather technical. The hon. member refers to a document "such as this". I have in my hand the "Canadian Economic Outlook for 1958", 31 pages long, mimeographed. He has asked me, is a document similar to that prepared? What does the hon. member mean? Does he mean 31 pages, of that size, and prepared by the economics branch? If that is what he means by the word "document", similar documents

are prepared because the economics branch continues to report to me and gives information which is, according to the foreword, "appraising the influences operating in the economy as they are likely to affect the general level of economic activity". Last night when I was making my opening remarks on the estimates I based them on similar reports given me by the economics branch and I laid before the house the outlook for the balance of 1960. That is the situation with regard to reports.
Let me follow that up. The document I understood the minister had reference to last night was the document "Public and private investment in Canada".

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: No.
Then when was the document given to the house? The point is that the minister gave his interpretation of some documents.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
No. I said that the outlook
report which I gave in the estimates speech last night was based on information supplied me by the economics branch of the Department of Trade and Commerce following along the same lines as is given in the foreword to this report "appraising the influences operating in the economy as they are likely to affect the general level of economic activity".

I regret I have not in front of me the Financial Post clipping, of which I have a very clear recollection as I am sure has also the minister. It was a report of a statement made by the head of his economics branch.
What date?
I will give that later in the debate. I also recall quite vividly that the headline was that a major recession was imminent in 1961-62.
That is what the Liberals would like.

No; this is from the senior representative of the economics branch of the Department of Trade and Commerce. I will get this clipping because I think the minister is aware of it. But in the course of this debate the minister should comment on that advice given to the nation at large, and doubtless given to the minister earlier, if we have not got in 1960 the usual concise report on economic prospects compiled by the innumerable economists which are employed by the Department of Trade and Commerce.

1 was interested, indeed somewhat amused, by the minister's historical explanation of the nature of the report used by the Prime Minister on the occasion to which we have been referring. The Prime Minister at that time said that this was a hidden report, that it was a horrible example of concealment on the part of the Liberals. According to Hansard for that year he said "It was hidden away so well we just found it".
Now the minister tells us that this was a report which was circulated from coast to coast, even to the Royal Military College, and therefore that the confidential character indicated by the cover had no meaning whatever. This was a report which the Prime Minister called a hidden report, so well concealed that even they could not find it in the first few weeks of their existence. Somebody must be wrong again.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: The Prime Minister mentioned the concealing of the facts contained in the report.
No, it is all on the record.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
On page 3525 of Hansard for 1958 he said:
They did not realize the situation or if they did so they concealed the facts from the Canadian people;-
And the report, the hidden report circulated from coast to coast.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
While we are still dealing with the economic report, if the Leader of the Opposition will look at page 7270 of Hansard for July 30 he might like to make some slight correction for the benefit of the house. He is reported as saying:
The Prime Minister took the confidential report, tore off the page marked "confidential",-
Earlier in 1958 when the hon. member for Ottawa West was discussing this report he mentioned the fact that the page had been torn off and someone asked him if he meant that the Prime Minister had torn it off, and the hon. member for Ottawa West was much more careful than the Leader of the Opposition, because he said "I have no evidence that was so". But here you have the Leader of the Opposition saying that the Prime Minister took the confidential report and tore off the page marked "confidential". I think that is a statement which should be corrected by the Leader of the Opposition.

Mr. Chairman, now the minister has brought it up the report was tabled by the Prime Minister with a part of the covering still on the report, with the word "confidential" left on that part. There was a report tabled by the Prime Minister himself and the report bore a bit of the covering 79951-0-488i
Supply-Trade and Commerce which had not been torn off. I have it here; the word "confidential" is marked on every page. If it will make the minister happier I will withdraw that word and say that the page with "confidential" marked on it was torn off.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: That makes it better.
I am glad to do that.

There can be no doubt that the Prime Minister did table a document that was confidential, that was hidden. Hansard volume IV, for the year 1957-58 at pages 3530, 3531, 3532 and 3533 clearly establishes that fact. What we are interested in now is in ascertaining from the government an indication of what lies ahead.
The Minister of Labour the other night said that there was no confidential document in the Department of Labour that was prepared for his assessment of the unemployment situation for the summer, for the fall or for the winter. However, after he was pressed he finally did admit that there was a confidential document, a confidential document that gave an estimate of the unemployment prospects for each quarter. However he refused to tell the committee even in general terms, what those prospects were. We insisted on having an indication of what the prospects were, so that we could determine if the government's unemployment program was vigorous enough to meet the situation which might eventuate.
We asked the Minister of Labour if there were any confidential surveys prepared in other departments which were made available to him; was the report of the governor of the Bank of Canada made available to him; did he know of any reports which were prepared for the benefit of the Minister of Finance; did he know of the economic surveys prepared for the Minister of Trade and Commerce? It was not possible to get from the Minister of Labour any acknowledgment as to whether these various departmental reports and the report of the Bank of Canada came across his desk, but he did finally admit there was a confidential report prepared for him in the Department of Labour, although he denied this in the course of the same debate the same evening.
Now we have before us today two contradictory statements by the Minister of Trade and Commerce. This is not my opinion. It is based on the record as I shall show. Now we are entitled to know from the Minister of Trade and Commerce if the prospects for trade are as indicated by the Leader of the Opposition. If the Leader of the Opposition is right, then obviously the enthusiasm about the prospects as stated by the Minister of Labour is incorrect. The Minister of Trade
7726	HOUSE OF
Supply-Trade and Commerce and Commerce can correct the statement made by the Minister of Labour as to the prospects for unemployment in the fall. We are now entitled to ask the Minister of Trade and Commerce on the basis of reports made to him annually in pursuit of a tradition, which has existed in that department for some time, to give us this information. There is no doubt that there was a report prepared known as the "Canadian Economic Outlook for 1957". The minister gave that in the house in January, 1958. We know there was a "Canadian Economic Outlook for 1959". The question now is: is there one for 1960 and if there is, on the basis of the policy of this government, that should now be considered as a public document, because the Prime Minister said there was no reason why it should not be given, and because there is no reason why it should not be given and for making it public, as he did in January, 1958-

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: A year later.

Never mind a year later. The Prime Minister said that confidential documents of that character should be given to the house. We want to know from the minister whether there is such a document, and because the Prime Minister has entered the chamber, I am going to give him the benefit of knowing the inconsistent position taken by the hon. minister. First of all, only a week ago, on July 30, as reported at page 7266 of Hansard, the following exchange took place:
In order to assist the committee of supply in considering the unemployment problem, will the Minister of Trade and Commerce table the "Canadian Economic Outlook for 1960"?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: If I am not mistaken, an order of the house was made with regard to this matter.
There was an order with respect to the volume for 1959, sir. Is the minister going to give an answer?

speakeroldname: Hon. Gordon Churchill (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
The hon. member for Bonavista-
Twillingate is asking for the tabling of a confidential report, and last evening the hon. member for Essex East said that this was contrary to the usages of parliament. I think perhaps we shall not do it.
First of all, before commenting on those words "I think perhaps we shall not do it", I shall deal with the statement I had made the previous day that such documents should not be made available.
