That is the position which I believe a responsible government should take; that is the position which the previous government took with regard to confidential documents.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: A responsible opposition should not ask for it.

But because the government does not regard this kind of confidential document, as we did, there can


be no excuse in logic or in fairness for refusing to table it. Here is the statement of the Minister of Trade and Commerce: "I think perhaps we shall not do it". That is what he said a week ago today in reply to the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate. That can only mean that there is such a document in existence for 1960.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: No.
It means there was a "Canadian Economic Outlook for 1960".

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: No, sir.

The minister says "no, sir". We shall deal with that answer in a few moments. The next day the minister said on Monday, August 1-but I will read the complete exchange:
Motion No. 136-Mr. Pickersgill:
For a copy of the "Canadian Economic Outlook for I960" prepared in the Department of Trade and Commerce.

speakeroldname: Hon. Gordon Churchill (Minister of Trade and Commerce) :
speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, there is no such document for 1960.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Does the hon. member wish his motion to be withdrawn?
Mr. Speaker, It seems to me there is no reason why the motion should not be passed. If there is no such document it obviously cannot be complied with.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on a point of order, it would not be in accordance with the practices and usages of parliament to pass a motion concerning a document which does not exist.
So the statement made by the minister on Monday, August 1 is inconsistent with the statement he made a few moments ago that there is no such document. But that is not what he said on Saturday, July 30 when he said: I think perhaps we shall not do it.
The position, now, I take it from the minister is that there is no "Economic Outlook for 1960" as such. I take it, since the minister does not disagree, that that is the position. Is the minister saying that his department does not give him any confidential statement or commentary on the economic picture for 1960? Is the minister saying he does not get it in some form? If that is the case, and if there is no such document, will the minister deny-

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: On a point of order, this is the most shocking repetition I have heard in ages. We have been all over this more than four times. All these questions were asked by the hon. member for Ottawa West, and I gave the answer. All the hon. member for Essex East is doing is getting into Hansard again as he has been for the last two weeks and putting on record things which are not correct. I have given the answers, and the hon. gentleman knows I have. This is repetition of the worst order.
The hon. gentleman is right-it is repetition, because it is directed at the minister in order to find out what the position is, since one position has been taken one day and denied the next.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Nonsense.

Because of these contradictions, and because so much is at stake, and because we have so much unemployment in this country we are entitled to know what kind of advice has been given to this government. That is the reason for this persistent interrogation. The Minister of Trade and Commerce is not going to halt me in this process-

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: On a question of privilege, Mr. Chairman, I will. On a question of privilege, I will halt the hon. member.
Does the minister have a point of order?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
I have a question of
privilege.
What is the question of privilege?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I thank the hon. member for Essex East very much. Now that the hon. member is acting as chairman of the committee and has asked for a statement from an hon. member, I will give it. My question of privilege is this. The hon. member for Essex East said I made a statement on July 30 and denied it on August 1. That statement or charge on the part of the hon. member for Essex East is false and should be withdrawn and I ask for its withdrawal right now.
All I am saying, Mr. Chairman, is that the minister said-
Withdraw.
Just a moment-
What about the bill of rights?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.

Mr. Chairman, in view of the fact that hon. gentlemen are attempting to shout me down, I should remind them that only recently we passed the bill of rights which surely means that we are entitled to speak-
It is no thanks to you that we passed the bill of rights, our bill.
It was improved by the hon. member for Essex East.

Mr. Chairman, perhaps my hon. friends think I have been unfair to the minister, and of course I would not want to be unfair to the hon. gentleman-
Supply-Trade and Commerce
Oh, oh.

-but if the minister has put before the house two contradictory positions I am certainly entitled to analyse them. On July 30 the hon. gentleman was asked by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate to produce or table the document called "Canadian Economic Outlook for 1960". As reported at page 7266 of Hansard of July 30 the Minister of Trade and Commerce said:
I think perhaps we shall not do it.
Now, how can you do it or how can you consider whether you should do it unless you have it?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: Nonsense.
Nonsense is no answer.
The Minister of Public Works displays an unusual eagerness today even for him-

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: The hon. member has been talking nonsense for the last half hour. During the course of his nonsense the hon. member asked a question. Does he want me to explain it?

The Minister of Public Works is a new minister. I do not want to be too hard on him, but I suggest that a new minister should always manage his own affairs, and having done that he should gradually learn to deal with matters affecting other departments. Returning to my point, the Minister of Trade and Commerce on July 30 with respect to the production of this document said:
X think perhaps we shall not do it.
But the very next day the minister said there was no such document. On August 1, as reported at page 7327 of Hansard, he said it would not be in accordance with the practice, having previously said that there was no such document for 1960. In the face of these two contradictions, Mr. Chairman, I suggest to you that the question of privilege raised by the hon. member is not one that really should have been raised.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I submit they are not contradictions.
If the minister would only explain these contradictions-

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: There are none.

If the minister would only say, "What I said on the first day was wrong," or "What I said on the second day was wrong," then the matter would be cleared up.
7728	HOUSE OF
Supply-Trade and Commerce

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: The hon. member for Essex East is wrong.

My hon. friend says I am wrong. I would remind the hon. gentleman that a mere assertion is no argument, and he waives an acknowledgement.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce is put in this dilemma. He finds himself imprisoned by his own contradictions. The reason he does not seek to extricate himself is because he has in his possession reports that back up the prognostications made by those gentlemen and those organizations referred to by the Leader of the Opposition.
And he will not give them to parliament.
One other reason for the minister refusing to produce these documents is because in revealing them, they will display the complete bankruptcy of the government's policy on unemployment.

Mr. Chairman, I always listen with rapt attention to the hon. member for Essex East and I always know that the louder the hon. gentleman talks and the more vociferous his delivery, the more uncertain he is of the facts. I am going to be generous to the hon. gentleman today-
Do not worry about me; be as severe as you can.
No, I will not be severe. I could not be severe to such a congenial hon. member.
And a very effective hon. member, too.

But I will say this. I follow a course of not answering the kind of things that are obviously untrue. From time to time in this house, as well as outside of it statements are made that in the days of Mr. Mackenzie King these were regarded as matters which were invariably raised by him on privilege. I have just had the opportunity of listening to the concluding remarks of the hon. gentleman. In view of the fact that he saw fit to quote some words that were spoken on July 30, the opportunity comes to me to answer those statements made on that occasion by the Leader of the Opposition who usually displays considerable courage in this regard in making statements unjustified by the facts, whenever I happen to be absent from the house.
Oh, oh.
Shameful.

The hon. gentleman has followed that course on a number of occasions and I agree with the hon. member for
[Mr. Martin (Essex East).)

Kenora-Rainy River that it is shameful to do that. The Leader of the Opposition made a statement the other day in reply to which I simply say to him that that statement was completely unjustified in any particular.
He is the most accurate speaker in the house.
Would the hon. gentleman not allow his spirits to overflow?
An unparliamentary remark.

I can understand how the Leader of the Opposition feels. I recall his experience on January 20, 1958. That was an historic day in the House of Commons. That was the day when the hon. gentleman produced that historic amendment-and I dislike to come back to this but I feel entitled to-that will never be forgotten in parliamentary history however many years this house of parliament may last. That was the day the hon, gentleman-
Are you still living in the past?
Living in the past? Hon. gentlemen do not like the past. When I refer to their part in it, they dislike that.
Let us look ahead.
It was my hon. friend the Leader of the Opposition who brought this up. I am going to recall that historic day for that memorable amendment deserves to be read.
The Prime Minister is out of order, but that is all right.

I do not want to cause the hon. gentleman and those associated with him any exacerbated feelings but I think it is only fair to refer to this in view of the fact that mention of this has been made and made in my absence. I therefore feel justified in saying a few words at this time.
By way of abuse of the rules.
Give us your speech over again.
Mr. Chairman, they do not like it.
We love it.
Mr. Meighen said he never abused the rules.
Hon. gentlemen opposite are hurt by their experience on that day. Let me read that famous amendment.
The hon. gentleman is quite out of order in doing so.

This was the amendment moved a few months after we came into power. It may be found at page 3520 of Hansard of January 20, 1958. On that occasion the Leader of the Opposition moved an amendment in these words:
That all the words after the word "That" be struck out and the following substituted therefor:
In view of the fact that, in the seven months His Excellency's advisers have been in office, Canada's total trade has ceased to expand, export markets have been threatened, and proposals for freer trade have been rebuffed-

Ask the
hon. member for Essex East about freer trade-

In the light of the experience of the two and a half years since, what of that statement regarding trade ceasing to expand, export markets being threatened and proposals for freer trade being rebuffed?
Half a million unemployed.
Oh, I will come to the unemployment question in a moment, but this gives me the opportunity, and I am glad of that opportunity, to deal with-
No one will suffer-
Incidentally, may I say this, that statement was never made.
Oh, oh.
I said that no person in this country will suffer from unemployment and we have seen that such has been the case.
Oh, oh.
Hear, hear.
Let me read on.
The worst unemployment in Canadian history.

Mr. Chairman, I sit and listen, I scarcely ever rise even to ask a question, but as soon as hon. gentlemen opposite realize that something may be said that they do not like they start this chattering. I simply ask that I be allowed to proceed without these aimless and inane interruptions.
Proceed, proceed.

I continue:
In view of the fact that, In the seven months ... Canada's total trade has ceased to expand, export markets have been threatened . .. that investment has been discouraged-
Hear, hear.

And so on I might go. Finally there are these words:
Supply-Trade and Commerce
And in view of the desirability, at this time, of having a government pledged to implement Liberal policies;
His Excellency's advisers should, in the opinion of this house, submit their resignation forthwith.
That is the best thing that could happen to Canada.
It would have been a good thing for the country.

I am just reading the record. I recall the Leader of the Opposition, on an occasion when there was some competition between him and the hon. member for Essex East, making a speech in which he said: "We want an election".
We do.

"We will be back in power and soon". While I listened to that from my bed I could just feel the fear that must have been in the hearts of those who were saying, "Resign, give us your place". Now, this is all on the record and they will never get over this amendment as long as time lasts, this monstrosity of an amendment. I do not think the Leader of the Opposition produced it on his own. He must have had help. I have always credited it to the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate.
Shame, shame.
If he is not entitled to the credit I withdraw the credit I have given him in this regard. They produced this thing and then it was 1958-
-and I produced the document-
Marked confidential.
-dealing with events in 1957, which in every particular contradicted in black and white the allegations made by hon. gentlemen opposite during 1957.
That is not so.
That happens to be untrue.
I went through the record. I do not want to reread it. If you want to read it-
You never did read it, you just took bits out of it.

I read it. Let me say this to the Leader of the Opposition. There was no removal of any part of that document. He made that statement in my absence and I say to him now in his presence that that statement is not in accordance with the facts. I am not going to go further than that so that there will be no misunderstanding, but I was very surprised. I can understand any

Supply-Trade and Commerce of the smaller folk surrounding him making statements like that but not the Leader of the Opposition. I was not here the other day, and if it had not been repeated today, I would not have thought it necessary to reply. I usually follow the course of not denying statements that are made from time to time for the reason that, after all, the denial never catches up with such a statement made without foundation by anyone. We talk about the course followed subsequently. I can understand how the souls of hon. gentlemen opposite have been seared.
Don't cry.

It has been so all through the ages. Caught out, it put them in a shameful position. They knew and the Leader of the Opposition knew in 1957 that we were entering a period of recession. The hon. member for Essex East knew.
Rubbish.
Mr. Harris referred to it in the budget.
They had been warned in the month of June of 1957, and if my recollection is correct the number of unemployed at that time was over 200,000.
One hundred and fifty thousand.
Your recollection is incorrect.
One hundred and fifty thousand; those are the facts.
Those are not the facts.
Show me the record.
Try to be accurate.
The record will show the situation and the position of affairs.
We will have the figures in a minute.
They knew this. They were warned. I am not going to read how they were warned but they knew and they concealed it. There is nothing that causes a person to be more outspoken than a guilty conscience.
Is that why you talk so much?

Yes, they concealed the facts. Then they sought refuge by endeavouring to make statements that were not based on the facts. In 1958 we had such a report; we produced it in 1959. So far as the 1959 report was concerned we were prepared to produce that report at the beginning of the next year. We made it perfectly clear that we would submit it in January, 1960, at the

beginning of the next year. We concealed nothing. Instead of accepting our promise and undertaking in that behalf, a vote was called and the house decided that that was not the time to secure the production of the document before the house. We were prepared to give them the 1959 report but hon. gentlemen opposite did not want to wait. They wanted it produced during the calendar year. We never produced any document during the calendar year. It was the year following. We were prepared to do that but they refused to accept it.
So far as the present situation is concerned, the Minister of Trade and Commerce has made it perfectly clear what is the situation. Hon. gentlemen opposite just gloat over the difficulties in the economic condition of Canada. They revel over the fact that there is a degree of unemployment. Wherever a market is lost through intensive international competition, they rub their hands in glee. That has been their attitude. I cannot understand it. I cannot conceive of an opposition made up of such fine gentlemen who would devote themselves so hopefully to the attainment of something in the nature of a depression in Canada. They are working to that end. They say-

Mr. Chairman, on a question of privilege, the Prime Minister of this country, without any respect for the dignity of his office, has said that the opposition is working for a depression in this country, which is a false, malicious slander and unworthy of him.
Mr. Chairman-
Perhaps he will withdraw it.
By their words ye shall know them. If they are not, and I believe the hon. gentleman says he is not, then he does not realize-
On a question of privilege, Mr. Chairman, I have asked that the Prime Minister withdraw those words.
Order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: "Honi soit qui mal y pense."

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: If I remember the words to which the Leader of the Opposition objects, there was a reference that the opposition was revelling-
No, no, Mr. Chairman.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
From what I heard, it would appear there was no question of privilege. A question of privilege has to be a matter which affects the conduct of an hon. member or his honour, and this seemed to

be a question of opinion as to attitude. In my opinion, there was no point of privilege in the statement made by the Prime Minister. After the Prime Minister has resumed his seat, the Leader of the Opposition may wish to make a correction if his attitude was not well represented in the remarks of the Prime Minister.
I am still speaking on the question of privilege, Mr. Chairman. Obviously you have not heard what the Prime Minister has said. He has just said that the oposition was working for a depression.
He did not.
Those were his words, and he cannot try to sneak out of them. Those words reflect on the opposition and therefore they should be withdrawn at once, and without any equivocation by the Prime Minister.
I do not know what the words were.
Well, I do.

Sometimes the hon. gentleman's recollections have not proven to be in accordance with the facts. I would say, if their sensibilities have been hurt, that if they are not working for it-I will not say they are because they tell me they are not-that will be the ultimate end as they go about this country preaching gloom and doom. I quite frankly say that they are not working for that purpose, but that will be the end, and that is what they are not unhopeful of obtaining.

On another question of
privilege, Mr. Chairman; I hope you heard those words. The Prime Minister has said that we are not unhopeful of a depression, and I ask the Prime Minister once again to withdraw at once words which are unworthy of him.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: May I say that in my opinion there is no question of privilege in those words.
No.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: If any hon. member wishes to refer the Chair to any citation in Beauchesne which would indicate that similar words would be sufficient to justify a question of privilege I am willing to examine the question further. I should like the Leader of the Opposition to refer me to any citation which would indicate that such words justify a question of privilege. I have no objection to examining the matter further.

The words used by the Prime Minister were that the opposition were not unhopeful of a depression in this country.
Supply-Trade and Commerce I call your attention to chapter 3, rules of debate, of Beauchesne's fourth edition, page 131:
No member can be allowed to attribute any intention to insult others; or
to question the honour of one;-
To tell the House of Commons that the opposition is not unhopeful for a depression in this country, with all that means to the people of this country, and to say that that is not a question of privilege or that is not insulting the opposition or questioning the honour of the opposition, seems to me to be incomprehensible. The Prime Minister should be asked at once to withdraw those words.
In that regard, I have nothing to withdraw.

The Leader of the Opposition has asked you, Mr. Chairman, on a point of order, to ask the hon. gentleman to withdraw a statement. Until you have been unequivocal in your ruling, it is not open to the Prime Minister to make any other argument.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The Prime Minister was answering the question of privilege which had been raised by the opposition, and gave his view as to whether those words should be withdrawn. This is the way I understood the intervention by the Prime Minister.

The Prime Minister has said he has nothing to withdraw in attributing to the opposition a desire for a depression or in saying that they were not unhopeful of a depression. Are you ruling, sir, that that is not a question of privilege and that the Prime Minister need not withdraw words of that kind?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I have not made any ruling as yet. I have been trying to find the citation to which the hon. member has referred me. Do I understand it is citation 155?
Yes.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
This is a citation which I have consulted several times. In my opinion what constitutes a matter of privilege is the imputation of false or unavowed motives or anything which concerns the personal conduct of an hon. member. In discussing problems generally, even if some expressions may be strong, in my view they would not justify a question of privilege because that is not something affecting the honour of any hon. member, and so no question of privilege would be involved.
Now, in so far as unparliamentary words are concerned, I think the rule is generally the same. There were no words used by the Prime Minister, in my opinion, that were unparliamentary. I do not see that there is a question of privilege. There may be justification, as I said before, for the Leader of

Supply-Trade and Commerce the Opposition to rise after the Prime Minister has completed his remarks and make a correction or state his views. Frankly I do not see that there is a question of privilege because neither the honour nor the conduct of the hon. member has been questioned.

According to your ruling, then, it is no reflection on the honour of the opposition for the Prime Minister to state that they are not unhopeful of a depression in this country. Is that your ruling, there is no question of privilege and no reflection on the honour of the opposition?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
May I refer the Leader of the Opposition to citation 150:
If a member should say nothing disrespectfully to the house or the Chair, or personally opprobrious to other members, or in violation of other rules of the house, he may state whatever he thinks fit in debate, however offensive it may be to the feelings, or injurious to the character, of individuals; and he is protected by his privilege from any action for libel, as well as from any other question or molestation.
If such a statement did justify a question of privilege, I think it would be very difficult to conduct the debates in this house. It is only what affects the personal conduct of hon. members that, in my opinion, justifies a question of privilege.
Then the only course open to me now that you have allowed the words of the Prime Minister to stand that the opposition is not unhopeful of a depression, is to say that this is a malicious falsehood.

Mr. Chairman, that is the usual course followed by the Leader of the Opposition. May I say to him that one of his most devoted followers was quoted in this house by the Minister of Finance on April 12. A Mr. Cohen was interviewing Mr. Templeton in the city of Toronto, and the following appears at page 3165 of Hansard for that date:
Mr. Templeton, I know that politics interest you. Off the record, do you see a revival on the federal scene of the Liberal party? Do you see them staging a comeback?
This is off the record on television?

Off the record on television.
Mr. Templeton then replied as follows:
The only thing I would say about that is that there is a chance of a Liberal revival if there is the economic recession predicted by-I hope accurately -by a number of well-known economists.
I need say no more in that connection.
You have said quite enough.
There was the spokesman-
You have branded yourself.

You will be charged.
[The Chairman.]
That was the statement on that. Now I return to the question of unemployment in 1957.

Mr. Chairman, the Prime Minister has quoted someone to substantiate his statement that the opposition of this house is not unhopeful of a depression. I call your attention to the fact that the Prime Minister has quoted no member of parliament in this house, no member of the opposition, and we were dealing with the question of the Prime Minister's statement about the opposition of this house. Of course, he was quite out of order in producing that statement.
No one challenged it.

As far as that is concerned, I can quite understand how the Leader of the Opposition feels in that regard, because after all, in the very beginning of our term of office, from the time that the famous amendment was moved in January, 1959-
It was our job.
-day after day, hour after hour in the house and outside the house they have continued to preach the probability, indeed the actual acceptance of recession in this house-
Hear, hear.

-and in many cases exaggerating the facts. They will object to my saying "for political purposes", and I certainly would want them to object properly to any statement that I make. I simply say that they exaggerated; they have overemphasized.
Give us the facts.
The hon. gentleman says "give us the facts". I am glad the hon. gentleman asked for the facts.
Six hundred thousand.
A moment ago he said there were one hundred and fifty-
And you said one hundred.
Sit down.
Sit down and hear the truth.
I have before me the news release-
Oh, oh.

The hon. member always laughs when he realizes he is in difficulty. The employment situation of June, 1957,

issued jointly by the Department of Labour and the dominion bureau of statistics shows that an estimated 5,834,000 persons had jobs on June 22, 1957. Registration for employment at N.E.S. offices-
Give us the figure. Mr. Chairman, on a point of order-
Sit down.
Mr. Chairman, on a point of order.
You do not want the facts now.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I see the hon. member for Essex East rising on a point of order.
The Prime Minister has challenged the figure which I gave.
No, no.
On a point of order-
No.
Mr. Chairman, you must-
Sit down.
Mr. Chairman, you must let me state my point of order. If the Prime Minister sits down, I will sit down with him.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I have to listen to the hon. member for Essex East.
I don't.
Mr. Chairman, you said you have to listen to me. I hope you do not mean it is a painful performance.
You said so.
The Prime Minister quoted-
Point of order. Sit down.
If the hon. gentleman wants me to put the facts before the house-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member for Essex East has risen on a point of order. I have to hear what he has to say to decide whether it is correct or not.
Thank you, Mr. Chairman. The Prime Minister was about to quote figures-
He has not quoted them yet.

I am sure hon. members opposite realize their difficulty; but surely they are going to allow me to plead at the bar of this house.
Supply-Trade and Commerce

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Does the hon. member sustain this point of order?
I was just addressing myself to these men who-
Order.

I made a statement as to the unemployed in June, 1957, and the Prime Minister now, in an effort to show that that was a wrong statement is quoting from the N.E.S. figures, which are not the figures on which I am relying, which he realizes. In order to be fair the Prime Minister ought to quote from the-
Order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. The Chair has heard enough to decide that this is not a point of order, but rather a point of disagreement.

Mr. Chairman, I know the hon. gentleman's great powers, but he does not yet know what I am going to read, although his powers of perception in this case indicate that he is afraid of the facts. Registration for employment at any N.E.S. offices-
How about persons without jobs?
-totalled about 267,000. I simply wanted to place on the record-
That is not the figure we were talking about, and you know it.

Mr. Chairman, that concludes what I have to say in this regard. I will conclude with the warning that the former government had in 1957. Coupled with that warning they proceeded throughout that entire election campaign to say that there was no unemployment, that all was well. Today their conscience is troubling them, and I can understand it. They concealed these facts from the Canadian people and they will never get over the fact that these concealed records, not made available in 1957, were shown in the house in 1958. We produced the 1958 economic report in 1959. We were prepared to produce the 1959 report in January, 1960, in accordance with the practice I followed in 1958. The opposition did not want it; they refused any delay and they asked for an immediate vote.
What about the 1960 figures?

As far as the present situation is concerned, the Minister of Trade and Commerce has stated, as I understand it, that there was no economic report of this type in 1960. There has been none. That is his statement and no amount of endeavour to obscure the issue-

Business of the House
What about what he said the day before?
Sit down.

-on the part of the opposition in any way answers what the Minister of Trade and Commerce has stated. We will give you the past reports; we will give you that report at any time up to 1959; but we do not intend to produce that which does not exist according to the minister.
Six o'clock.
Mr. Chairman, I wonder if the Prime Minister-
Six o'clock.
You called it, so sit down.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Some hon. members have called it six o'clock. Shall I rise, report resolutions and ask leave to sit again?
Progress reported.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wonder if the house leader would like to sit tonight in order to make further progress with his estimates?
No.
We might as well sit here till September now.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I think not. In view of the exhaustion apparent on the other side I think we should rise.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I would think the exhaustion is on the other side, judging from the noise we have had. Could we get some indication of what we will be doing next week, particularly on Monday, and would the house leader be good enough to indicate the order in which these items will be taken?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: We have a few items left, as I mentioned last night, to consider and they will come up on Monday. There is the concurrence in the report of the civil service commission affecting the staff of the House of Commons; the concurrence in the report of the committee on procedure, and various other items to which I drew attention last night.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: May I ask if these items will be taken in the order in which they were given last night?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
I think that will be the order in which we will take things on Monday. If there should be any change in that order I will notify hon. members on the other side in plenty of time prior to the opening of the house at 3 p.m. on Monday afternoon.
The house adjourned at six o'clock, without question put, pursuant to special order.
